docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Generated by Nikhil Kumar Rajput

A plain-English map of the attacks that threaten computers, networks and people: how they are classified, how each works, the incidents that made them famous and the defences that work.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Active and Passive Attacks
docs.text: All cyber attacks can be sorted into two broad families according to what the attacker does: active attacks, which change or disrupt something, and passive attacks, which only watch. This chapter sets out the whole taxonomy in one picture, then walks through six active and six passive attacks. The distinction matters because it dictates the defence. Active attacks are noisy and the victim may notice; passive attacks leave no trace, so the only sound defence is prevention, above all encryption.

docs.title: 1.1 Two families of attack
docs.text:
Cyber attacks can be organised along four axes, and the same attack appears on several of them. By behaviour an attack is active or passive. By target layer it is aimed at the network, a web application, an operating system or the radio link. By technique it is malware, phishing, social engineering, a password attack or a denial of service. By actor it comes from an insider, through a supply chain or from an advanced persistent threat. The chapters of this book follow these axes in turn; Figure 1.1 shows the whole map. This chapter takes the first axis, which is the most basic.

Figure 1.1. A map of cyber attacks along four axes: attacker behaviour, target layer, technique and actor.

The two families of the first axis are easy to tell apart, as Figure 1.2 shows. The test is whether the attacker changes anything.

Figure 1.2. In a passive attack the data reaches the receiver unchanged while the attacker copies it; in an active attack the attacker sits in the path and alters, injects, replays or blocks data.

docs.title: Active attacks
docs.text:
In an active attack, the attacker actively modifies data, disrupts systems, or interacts directly with the target. The victim may notice something is wrong.

Layman analogy

Like a burglar who breaks into your house, moves things around, steals items, and possibly vandalizes the place. The disruption is visible.

docs.title: Passive attacks
docs.text:
In a passive attack, the attacker only observes and collects information without modifying anything. The victim usually has no idea anything happened.

Layman analogy

Like a spy who secretly copies a key, enters your house while you're away, photographs every document, and leaves without touching anything. You'd never know they were there.

docs.title: 1.2 DoS / DDoS — Denial of Service
docs.text:
The attacker overwhelms a system with so much traffic or so many requests that it can no longer serve legitimate users.

Example: Imagine 1 million people all trying to call one phone number at the same time. The line is completely jammed and no real calls get through.

Example 1.1: DoS / DDoS — Denial of Service

The 2016 Dyn DNS attack used the Mirai botnet (600,000 infected IoT devices) to flood the DNS provider with 1.2 terabits per second of traffic, taking down Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, and Spotify for millions of users.

docs.title: 1.3 Man-in-the-Middle (MitM)
docs.text:
The attacker secretly intercepts and alters communications between two parties. Neither party knows the attacker is present.

Layman analogy

Like a corrupt postman who opens your sealed letters, reads them, changes some of the content, reseals the envelopes, and delivers them. Both sender and receiver are unaware.

Example 1.2: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM)

Attackers on public Wi-Fi networks intercept banking sessions, reading and sometimes altering the data passing between users and their banks.

docs.title: 1.4 Session Hijacking
docs.text:
After a user logs in to a website, the server issues a "session token" (like a VIP wristband proving you paid entry). The attacker steals this token and uses it to impersonate the user without needing a password.

Layman analogy

You check into a hotel and get a keycard. Someone steals your keycard while you're sleeping and uses it to access your room and the hotel's facilities as if they were you.

docs.title: 1.5 SQL Injection
docs.text:
The attacker inserts malicious database commands into an input field (like a search box or login form), tricking the system into executing them.

Layman analogy

A restaurant takes orders verbally. If you say "Give me a burger, AND also read out all customer credit card numbers," a naive system might comply.

Example 1.4: SQL Injection

In 2009, Heartland Payment Systems was hit with SQL injection, exposing 130 million credit card numbers — the largest data breach at the time, costing $140 million in settlements.

docs.title: 1.6 Ransomware
docs.text:
The attacker encrypts all the victim's files and demands a ransom payment (usually in cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key.

Layman analogy

Someone breaks into your house, changes every single lock — on every door, drawer, and cabinet — and leaves a note: "Pay $10,000 in Bitcoin for the master key."

Example 1.5: Ransomware

The Colonial Pipeline attack (2021): DarkSide ransomware shut down the largest US fuel pipeline for 6 days. The company paid $4.4 million ransom, causing fuel shortages across the US East Coast.

docs.title: 1.7 Replay Attack
docs.text:
The attacker captures a valid authentication message (like a login token) and retransmits it later to gain unauthorized access, without ever knowing the actual password.

Layman analogy

You record the exact secret knock used to enter a private club. Later, you play the recording at the door and get let in — because the doorman only checks the knock pattern, not who's doing it.

docs.title: 1.8 Packet Sniffing
docs.text:
The attacker captures raw data packets traveling over a network. On unencrypted networks, this reveals everything: passwords, emails, browsing history, credit card numbers.

Layman analogy

Like using a radio scanner to listen to unencrypted walkie-talkie conversations. If the signal isn't scrambled (encrypted), you can hear everything.

Common tool: Wireshark (free, open-source, widely used by both attackers and legitimate network engineers).

docs.title: 1.9 Eavesdropping
docs.text:
Listening in on VoIP (voice-over-internet) calls, unencrypted chat messages, or other communications as they travel across the network.

Layman analogy

Sitting in a coffee shop next to someone having a private phone call. If they're talking loudly in public, you hear everything.

docs.title: 1.10 Traffic Analysis
docs.text:
Even if data is encrypted (unreadable), analyzing the patterns of communication reveals useful information: who talks to whom, how often, how much data is sent, and when.

Layman analogy

You can't read sealed letters, but if you notice someone sends 50 letters a day to a specific law firm, that pattern alone tells you they're probably in legal trouble.

docs.title: 1.11 War Driving
docs.text:
Driving through neighbourhoods with a laptop and wireless antenna to discover, map, and catalogue unsecured Wi-Fi networks for later exploitation.

Layman analogy

Driving slowly through a neighbourhood, testing every doorknob to see which houses have unlocked doors — noting addresses for later.

docs.title: 1.12 Shoulder Surfing
docs.text:
Physically watching someone enter their PIN or password — at an ATM, in a coffee shop, or on public transport.

Layman analogy

Standing behind someone at an ATM and memorising the numbers they press. Old technique, still devastatingly effective.

docs.title: 1.13 Dumpster Diving
docs.text:
Searching through discarded rubbish for sensitive information: old invoices, contracts, printed passwords, employee lists, or hardware containing stored data.

Layman analogy

Going through someone's bin after they've thrown out bank statements, medical records, or a Post-it note with their passwords written on it.

docs.title: 1.14 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Encrypt all network traffic — use HTTPS websites and a VPN on public Wi-Fi
  • Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on all important accounts
  • Shred all sensitive documents before discarding — never throw them in general waste
  • Be aware of your surroundings when entering PINs or passwords in public
  • Use end-to-end encrypted messaging apps (Signal, WhatsApp) for sensitive conversations

docs.title: 1.15 Summary
docs.text:
• Attacks are classified by behaviour (active or passive), by target layer, by technique and by actor. Learning the families lets you recognise new variants.
  • Active attacks modify data or disrupt systems and may be noticed: DoS, man-in-the-middle, session hijacking, SQL injection, ransomware and replay.
  • Passive attacks only observe: packet sniffing, eavesdropping, traffic analysis, war driving, shoulder surfing and dumpster diving. The victim usually never knows.
  • Passive attacks can only be prevented, not detected, which is why encryption (HTTPS, VPN, end-to-end messaging) is the first defence.

docs.title: 1.16 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Classify each as an active or a passive attack: (a) packet sniffing, (b) session hijacking, (c) traffic analysis, (d) replay attack, (e) shoulder surfing, (f) ransomware.

    Answer

    (a) Passive. (b) Active. (c) Passive. (d) Active, because the attacker retransmits captured data. (e) Passive. (f) Active. The test is whether the attacker modifies or disrupts something or only observes.

  2. Explain how traffic analysis can reveal useful information even though the content is encrypted.

    Answer

    Encryption hides the content but not who is talking to whom, how often, how much data is sent and when. Fifty messages a day to a law firm suggests legal trouble whatever they say.

  3. Why can a passive attack almost never be detected by its victim, and what does that imply about the best defence?

    Answer

    The attacker changes nothing, so no log entry, error or slowdown appears. Detection is therefore unreliable, and the defence must be preventive: encrypt traffic, shred documents, and be careful where you type PINs and passwords.

  4. How does a replay attack differ from stealing a password? Why does it work?

    Answer

    The attacker never learns the password. A valid authentication message is captured and retransmitted later. It works when the receiving side checks only that the message is valid, not that it is fresh, like a doorman who checks the knock pattern and not who is knocking.

  5. Pair each defence with the attack it mainly addresses: (i) shredding documents, (ii) HTTPS or a VPN, (iii) multi-factor authentication, (iv) end-to-end encrypted messaging. Attacks: dumpster diving, packet sniffing on public Wi-Fi, eavesdropping on conversations, stolen session or password.

    Answer

    (i) Dumpster diving. (ii) Packet sniffing on public Wi-Fi. (iii) A stolen session or password, because a second factor makes the stolen credential insufficient. (iv) Eavesdropping on conversations.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Advanced Persistent Threats
docs.text:
An advanced persistent threat is a long, patient, well-resourced operation, typically by a nation-state or a group it sponsors. "Advanced" refers to the techniques, "persistent" to the months or years of undetected access, and "threat" to the strategic consequences. This chapter describes the six phases of the APT kill chain and four well-known groups, and shows why defence against APTs rests on behavioural detection rather than on any single product.

Layman analogy

An APT is not a smash-and-grab burglary. It's a highly trained, highly patient spy who spends months building a cover identity, gets a legitimate job at your organisation, slowly earns trust, gains access to the most sensitive areas, meticulously photographs every document over 18 months, and departs quietly — with no one ever suspecting they were anything other than a loyal employee.

docs.title: 12.1 The kill chain in six phases
docs.text: Figure 12.1. The six phases of an APT kill chain.

docs.title: Phase 1: Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Gather comprehensive intelligence on the target organisation before any attack begins.

  • OSINT (Open Source Intelligence): LinkedIn profiling, company websites, DNS records, WHOIS data
  • Email harvesting: Collect employee email addresses to identify spear phishing targets
  • Social media analysis: Map the org chart, identify executives, IT staff, travel patterns, and relationships
  • Goal: Build a detailed picture of the target before firing a single packet

docs.title: Phase 2: Initial Access
docs.text:
Gain the first, carefully concealed foothold inside the target environment.

  • Spear phishing: Highly targeted email to a specific, researched individual with a relevant malicious document
  • Zero-day exploit: Use an unpatched vulnerability in software the target uses
  • Watering hole attack: Compromise a website the target's employees are known to visit regularly

docs.title: Phase 3: Establish Foothold
docs.text:
Ensure persistent access that survives reboots, password changes, and partial detection.

  • Install a backdoor that automatically re-establishes itself after reboots
  • Implant a C2 (Command and Control) beacon — a hidden process that regularly "checks in" with the attacker's server
  • Establish multiple redundant access paths in case one is discovered and closed

docs.title: Phase 4: Escalate Privileges
docs.text:
Move from the initial low-privilege access to administrator or domain administrator level.

  • Exploit local OS vulnerabilities to gain elevated privileges
  • Mimikatz: A well-known tool that extracts plaintext passwords and hashes from Windows memory
  • Kerberoasting: Extract service account password hashes from Active Directory and crack them offline

docs.title: Phase 5: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Spread from the initial compromised machine to other systems across the network, moving towards high-value targets.

  • Pass-the-Hash: Use captured password hashes to authenticate without ever knowing the plaintext password
  • RDP Pivoting: Use Remote Desktop Protocol to hop between internal machines
  • Living-off-the-Land: Use legitimate Windows built-in tools (PowerShell, WMI, PsExec) to avoid triggering antivirus

docs.title: Phase 6: Data Exfiltration
docs.text:
Extract the target data covertly over an extended period, avoiding detection.

  • Compress and encrypt all target data before exfiltration to minimise size and evade content inspection
  • Stage data in obscure internal locations before slowly moving it outward
  • Exfiltrate gradually over months via covert channels: DNS tunnelling, HTTPS to legitimate cloud services

docs.title: 12.2 Notable APT Groups
docs.text:
APT29 — "Cozy Bear" (Russia / SVR): SolarWinds supply chain attack, 2016 DNC hack, COVID-19 vaccine research theft. Techniques: spear phishing, supply chain attacks, stealthy C2 via legitimate cloud services. Targets: government, defence, healthcare.

APT41 — "Double Dragon" (China / MSS): Conducts both government-directed espionage AND financially motivated cybercrime simultaneously — a rare dual mandate. Targets healthcare, gaming, telecommunications. Uses zero-days, watering holes, and ransomware.

Lazarus Group (North Korea / RGB): $1.3B in cryptocurrency theft, $81M Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist, WannaCry ransomware, Sony Pictures hack. Primarily financially motivated — generates hard currency to fund the North Korean regime in defiance of international sanctions.

APT33 — "Elfin" (Iran / IRGC): Saudi Aramco (Shamoon wiper malware destroyed 35,000 computers), US aerospace companies, global energy sector. Specialises in destructive wiper malware designed to erase and permanently destroy data.

docs.title: 12.3 The four groups at a glance
docs.text: Group Origin (as reported) Notable activity Typical techniques APT29 (Cozy Bear) Russia (SVR) SolarWinds, the 2016 DNC hack, theft of COVID-19 vaccine research Spear phishing, supply chain, stealthy C2 through legitimate cloud services APT41 (Double Dragon) China (MSS) Espionage and financially motivated crime at once, in healthcare, gaming and telecommunications Watering holes, zero-days, ransomware Lazarus Group North Korea (RGB) About $1.3 billion of cryptocurrency theft, the $81 million Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist, WannaCry, the Sony Pictures hack Supply chain, attacks on the SWIFT network APT33 (Elfin) Iran (IRGC) Saudi Aramco (Shamoon wiper malware), US aerospace, the energy sector Spear phishing, wiper malware

docs.title: 12.4 Defence tips
docs.text:
• APTs bypass traditional antivirus — behavioural detection (EDR) is essential
  • Implement Zero Trust architecture — verify every access request, trust no one by default
  • Network segmentation — a breach of one segment cannot automatically reach others
  • Subscribe to threat intelligence feeds: MITRE ATT&CK framework, CISA advisories, FBI flash alerts
  • Hunt proactively — actively search for indicators of compromise rather than waiting for alerts
  • Log everything — comprehensive logging is essential for post-breach forensic investigation
  • Practice and test your incident response plan before you need it — not during a crisis

docs.title: 12.5 Summary
docs.text:
• An APT is advanced, persistent and a threat; it unfolds in six phases: reconnaissance, initial access, foothold, privilege escalation, lateral movement and exfiltration.
  • APTs use living-off-the-land tools and covert channels so that antivirus sees nothing wrong.
  • APT29, APT41, Lazarus Group and APT33 illustrate different motives: espionage, mixed espionage and crime, revenue for a state, and destruction.
  • Defence is behavioural: EDR, Zero Trust, segmentation, threat intelligence, proactive hunting, full logging and a rehearsed incident-response plan.

docs.title: 12.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Put these in order: lateral movement, data exfiltration, reconnaissance, establish foothold, escalate privileges, initial access.

    Answer

    Reconnaissance, initial access, establish foothold, escalate privileges, lateral movement, data exfiltration.

  2. Explain the three words of "advanced persistent threat".

    Answer

    Advanced: cutting-edge techniques. Persistent: access maintained for months or years without detection. Threat: serious, strategic consequences, such as espionage or sabotage.

  3. What does "living off the land" mean and why does it defeat antivirus?

    Answer

    The attacker uses legitimate built-in tools (PowerShell, WMI, PsExec) instead of custom malware. Antivirus has nothing to flag because the programs are the system's own, so only behavioural detection can notice the misuse.

  4. At which kill-chain phase would (a) user training, (b) network segmentation and (c) monitoring for unusual outbound DNS or cloud uploads help most?

    Answer

    (a) Initial access, where spear phishing is the usual entry. (b) Lateral movement, because a breach of one segment cannot automatically reach others. (c) Data exfiltration.

  5. Why do APTs exfiltrate data slowly over months through channels such as DNS tunnelling?

    Answer

    Slow transfers through normal-looking channels stay below detection thresholds and blend with legitimate traffic, so the theft is not noticed.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Defence Principles and Key Takeaways
docs.text: Understanding attacks is only half the equation. This chapter gathers the defences from all the earlier chapters into six principles: identity is the new perimeter, assume breach, patch fast, visibility equals detection equals response, humans are the first attack vector, and supply-chain trust must be verified. If you remember only six sentences from this book, remember these.

docs.title: 13.1 Identity Is the New Perimeter
docs.text:
Traditional security assumed: "inside the corporate network = trusted." With cloud computing, remote work, mobile devices, and third-party services, this assumption is completely broken. Your "perimeter" is now every identity credential in your organisation.

Modern Principle: ZERO TRUST — "Never trust, always verify." Treat every access request — regardless of where it comes from, inside or outside the network — as potentially hostile until verified.

  • Enable MFA on every single account, without exception
  • Adopt Passkeys (FIDO2) where possible — cryptographically phishing-resistant
  • Assume credentials will eventually be stolen — make stolen credentials useless without the second factor

docs.title: 13.2 Assume Breach Mentality
docs.text:
The question is not "Will we be breached?" but "When we are breached, how quickly can we detect it, contain it, and recover from it?" Build your defences assuming the attacker is already inside.

  • Zero Trust architecture — no implicit trust anywhere on the network
  • Least privilege access — users and systems get the minimum permissions required
  • Network segmentation — a breach of one area cannot automatically spread to all others
  • Regular penetration testing — find your weaknesses before attackers do
  • Incident response planning and drills — practised response is ten times faster than improvised response

docs.title: 13.3 Patch Fast
docs.text:
FACT: Studies consistently show that 60% of successful breaches exploit known vulnerabilities for which a patch was already available but had not been applied.

The moment a security patch is released, attackers reverse-engineer it to understand the underlying vulnerability and immediately target all systems that haven't yet applied the fix. The window between patch release and active exploitation is often measured in hours, not weeks.

  • Implement automated patch management for all systems
  • Vulnerability scanning: continuously identify unpatched systems
  • Establish an emergency patching process for critical CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
  • Include third-party software and firmware — not just the OS

docs.title: 13.4 Visibility = Detection = Response
docs.text:
You cannot defend what you cannot see. You cannot respond to what you haven't detected. Comprehensive visibility across your entire environment is the foundation of effective defence.

  • SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) — centralised log collection and automated correlation
  • EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) — behavioural monitoring on every laptop, server, and device
  • NDR (Network Detection and Response) — monitor and analyse all network traffic for anomalies
  • SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) — automate responses to common, known threats

docs.title: 13.5 Humans are the first attack vector
docs.text:
FACT: 91% of all cyberattacks begin with a phishing email or other human manipulation. The most sophisticated technical security controls can be — and regularly are — rendered completely ineffective by a single employee clicking a single malicious link.

  • Regular, engaging security awareness training — not annual checkbox exercises that are immediately forgotten
  • Phishing simulation exercises with immediate, constructive feedback
  • Clear, simple reporting procedures for suspicious emails, calls, and requests
  • Create a culture where employees feel safe reporting mistakes without fear of punishment
  • Measure and track the human risk across the organisation

docs.title: 13.6 Supply Chain Trust Must Be Verified
docs.text:
FACT: The SolarWinds attack proved that your most trusted, most established software tools can be your biggest security risk. Every dependency, every vendor, every update is a potential attack vector.

  • Audit third-party vendor security posture before granting access
  • Maintain a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — know every component in your software stack
  • Verify software integrity via cryptographic checksums before deploying updates
  • Limit and monitor all third-party access — grant minimum necessary access only

Final thought

Security is not a product you buy or a project you complete — it is a continuous process of awareness, vigilance, and adaptation. The threat landscape evolves every day. Defenders must evolve with it.

docs.title: 13.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Identity is the new perimeter: MFA everywhere, passkeys where possible, and Zero Trust (never trust, always verify).
  • Assume breach: least privilege, segmentation, penetration testing and rehearsed incident response.
  • Patch fast: attackers reverse-engineer patches within hours; include firmware and third-party software.
  • Visibility equals detection equals response (SIEM, EDR, NDR, SOAR); humans are the first vector (training, simulations, a no-blame reporting culture); supply-chain trust must be verified (vendor audits, SBOM, checksums).

docs.title: 13.8 Exercises
docs.text:
1. State the Zero Trust principle in one sentence and say what it replaces.

    Answer

    Never trust, always verify: every access request is treated as potentially hostile until verified, wherever it comes from. It replaces the older assumption that anything inside the corporate network is trusted.

  2. What does "assume breach" change in the way defences are designed?

    Answer

    The question shifts from whether an attacker will get in to how quickly the breach will be detected, contained and recovered from. That means least privilege, segmentation, regular testing and rehearsed incident response.

  3. Why is MFA not a complete defence against phishing, and what is?

    Answer

    A real-time reverse-proxy phishing tool (such as Modlishka) can relay the victim's one-time code as it is typed. FIDO2 passkeys are bound to the real domain and cannot be relayed to a fake one.

  4. Expand SIEM, EDR, NDR and SOAR and say what each contributes to "visibility equals detection equals response".

    Answer

    SIEM: Security Information and Event Management, central log collection and correlation. EDR: Endpoint Detection and Response, behavioural monitoring of devices. NDR: Network Detection and Response, analysis of network traffic. SOAR: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response, automating the response to known threats.

  5. Map each attack to the principle that addresses it most directly: credential stuffing, SolarWinds, exploitation of a known CVE months after its patch, ransomware that spreads from one workstation.

    Answer

    Credential stuffing: identity is the new perimeter (unique passwords and MFA). SolarWinds: supply-chain trust must be verified. Exploitation of a known CVE: patch fast. Ransomware spreading from one workstation: assume breach (segmentation and least privilege).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Denial of Service in Depth
docs.text:
Denial-of-service attacks do not steal anything. They make a service unavailable by overwhelming it. Chapter 2 introduced them briefly; this chapter looks at them in depth, sorted into three categories according to what they exhaust: bandwidth, server and network-equipment resources, or a single application. It also lists the record-setting attacks of the last decade, which show how fast the scale has grown.

Layman analogy

DoS is one person lying across the entrance to a shop, blocking everyone from entering. DDoS is 50,000 people simultaneously blocking every entrance, exit, window, and ventilation shaft of an entire building.

docs.title: 8.1 DoS vs DDoS
docs.text:
• DoS — single source; relatively easy to block by filtering that one IP address
  • DDoS — thousands or millions of sources (compromised botnet); nearly impossible to block by IP filtering alone

docs.title: 8.2 Volume-Based Attacks — Saturate Bandwidth
docs.text:
Flood the target with so much traffic that their internet connection is completely saturated.

UDP Flood: Spoofs the source IP address and sends UDP packets to all ports on the target. The server attempts to respond to every packet, consuming all available resources.

ICMP Flood (Ping Flood): Overwhelms the target with ICMP echo request (ping) packets at massive volume.

DNS Amplification: Send a small DNS request (with the victim's IP as the spoofed source) to public DNS servers. The DNS server sends a response up to 50x larger in size back to the victim. The attacker generates massive traffic while sending relatively little.

Layman analogy

You call a stranger, pretend to be your target, and request a 50-page fax be sent to the target's number. The fax machine (DNS server) sends 50 pages to the victim (target). The attacker barely did any work.

NTP Amplification: Uses Network Time Protocol servers which can respond with up to 556x the size of the request — the highest amplification ratio of any DDoS technique.

docs.title: 8.3 Protocol-Based Attacks — Exhaust Server Resources
docs.text:
Exploit weaknesses in network protocols to exhaust server memory, CPU, or connection tables.

SYN Flood: Exploits the TCP three-way handshake. The attacker sends thousands of SYN (connection initiation) packets but never sends the final ACK to complete the connection. The server allocates memory for each half-open connection and waits, eventually exhausting its connection table.

Ping of Death: Sends malformed, oversized ICMP packets that crash vulnerable systems when they attempt to reassemble them.

Smurf Attack: Broadcasts an ICMP request to an entire network using the victim's IP as the spoofed source. Every device on the network replies to the victim, multiplying the attack traffic.

docs.title: 8.4 Application Layer Attacks — Target Specific Services
docs.text:
Mimic legitimate user behaviour to exhaust application-specific resources. These use lower traffic volumes and are much harder to distinguish from normal usage.

HTTP Flood: Sends massive numbers of legitimate-looking HTTP GET or POST requests to a web server until it cannot process any more.

Slowloris: Opens thousands of HTTP connections to the server simultaneously, then sends data extremely slowly — just enough to keep each connection alive. The server waits for each request to complete, eventually exhausting its maximum concurrent connections.

RUDY (R-U-Dead-Yet): Sends HTTP POST requests with an extremely large, declared Content-Length, then drip-feeds the body one byte at a time, tying up server threads indefinitely.

docs.title: 8.5 Notable Real-World DDoS Attacks
docs.text:
• 2016 — Dyn DNS: 1.2 Tbps via Mirai botnet. Took down Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, Spotify, CNN.
  • 2018 — GitHub: 1.35 Tbps via memcached amplification — at the time the largest DDoS ever recorded.
  • 2020 — AWS Shield: 2.3 Tbps — surpassed GitHub to become the new record.
  • 2022 — Google Cloud: 46 million requests per second (RPS) HTTPS flood from thousands of sources — the largest application-layer attack recorded at that time.

docs.title: 8.6 How the three categories compare
docs.text:
Figure 8.1. The three categories of DoS and DDoS attack, what each exhausts, and examples.

The categories also differ in how they are measured and how they are stopped. Volume is measured in bits per second and is answered with capacity, by mitigation services, content delivery networks and traffic scrubbing. Protocol attacks are answered by making the stack stateless where it can be (SYN cookies). Application-layer attacks are measured in requests per second and are the hardest to distinguish from real users, so they need rate limits, connection limits and behavioural analysis.

docs.title: 8.7 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Subscribe to DDoS mitigation services: Cloudflare, AWS Shield, Akamai, Imperva
  • Implement rate limiting and connection limits at the network edge
  • Configure SYN cookies to defend against SYN flood attacks without storing half-open connections
  • Use anycast network routing to distribute attack traffic across multiple datacentres
  • Use Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to absorb volumetric attacks
  • Enable traffic scrubbing for enterprise environments

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
• DoS comes from one source and is easy to block; DDoS comes from thousands of sources and cannot be stopped by blocking addresses.
  • Volume-based attacks saturate bandwidth (amplification multiplies the traffic 50 to 556 times); protocol-based attacks exhaust state (SYN flood); application-layer attacks mimic users (Slowloris, RUDY, HTTP flood).
  • Records have risen from 1.2 Tbps in 2016 to 2.3 Tbps in 2020, and application-layer attacks reached 46 million requests per second in 2022.
  • Defences: mitigation services, rate limiting, SYN cookies, anycast, CDNs and scrubbing.

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why does blocking a single IP address stop a DoS attack but not a DDoS attack?

    Answer

    In a DoS attack all the traffic comes from one source, so blocking it ends the attack. A DDoS attack comes from thousands or millions of bots, so there is no single address to block, and the sources are legitimate-looking machines.

  2. NTP amplification can respond with up to 556 times the size of the request. How much traffic does an attacker's 2 Mbit/s of spoofed requests produce at the victim?

    Answer

    \(2\times556=1112\) Mbit/s, about 1.1 Gbit/s.

  3. Why are application-layer attacks harder to detect than volume-based ones?

    Answer

    They use lower traffic volumes and mimic legitimate user behaviour, so they do not trip bandwidth alarms and cannot easily be told from a busy day.

  4. Explain how Slowloris ties up a web server.

    Answer

    It opens thousands of HTTP connections and sends data very slowly, just enough to keep each one alive. The server waits for each request to complete and eventually reaches its maximum number of concurrent connections, so real users are refused.

  5. Name four defences against DDoS attacks and the category each helps most with.

    Answer

    Mitigation services, CDNs and traffic scrubbing absorb volume-based attacks. SYN cookies defend against protocol-based attacks such as SYN floods. Rate limiting and connection limits at the edge help against application-layer attacks. Anycast routing spreads attack traffic across several data centres.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
A quick reference to the technical terms used in the book.

APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) A sophisticated, long-duration cyberattack — typically by a nation-state — focused on stealthily maintaining access to a target for months or years to steal data or conduct espionage. ARP Poisoning Sending false ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) messages to associate the attacker's MAC address with a legitimate IP, causing traffic to be redirected through the attacker. Authentication The process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or system before granting access. Passwords, PINs, biometrics, and hardware tokens are all forms of authentication. Botnet A network of malware-infected computers ("bots") controlled remotely by an attacker's Command-and-Control server, often without the owners' knowledge. Brute Force Systematically attempting every possible password or key combination until the correct one is found. Buffer Overflow Writing more data to a memory buffer than it can hold, causing the overflow to overwrite adjacent memory and potentially redirect program execution to attacker-controlled code. C2 / C&C (Command and Control) The infrastructure (server, domain, or channel) used by an attacker to remotely control malware or compromised systems in a botnet. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) An attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into making unauthorised requests to a trusted site the user is already logged into. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) A standardised identifier for publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Example: CVE-2021-4034 is the PwnKit Linux privilege escalation vulnerability. DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) An attack using multiple sources (often a botnet) to flood a target with traffic, making it unavailable to legitimate users. DLL (Dynamic Link Library) A shared code module in Windows that multiple programs load and use. DLL hijacking places a malicious DLL where it is loaded instead of the legitimate one. DNS (Domain Name System) The internet's "phone book" — translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into IP addresses that computers use to communicate. DoS (Denial of Service) An attack from a single source that overwhelms a target system, making it unavailable to legitimate users. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) Security software that continuously monitors devices (endpoints) for suspicious behaviour, detecting attacks that traditional antivirus misses (including fileless malware and APTs). Encryption The process of transforming readable data (plaintext) into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using a mathematical algorithm. Only those with the correct key can decrypt it. Exploit A piece of code or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability (a weakness in software, hardware, or configuration) to cause unintended behaviour. FIDO2 / Passkey A modern, phishing-resistant authentication standard. Authentication is cryptographically bound to the specific website domain — fake sites cannot trigger it. No password is ever transmitted. Firewall A security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules, creating a barrier between trusted and untrusted networks. Hash A one-way cryptographic transformation of data into a fixed-length string. Passwords are stored as hashes — the original password cannot be mathematically recovered from the hash alone. HTTP / HTTPS HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the protocol for web communication. HTTPS is the encrypted version using TLS/SSL. Always look for HTTPS (the padlock) before entering sensitive information. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) A web vulnerability where an application exposes internal object identifiers (like database IDs) without verifying that the requesting user is authorised to access that specific object. IoT (Internet of Things) Network-connected physical devices beyond traditional computers: smart TVs, security cameras, routers, thermostats, industrial sensors. Often have weak default security configurations. IP Address A unique numerical label assigned to every device on a network, enabling communication between devices. Like a postal address for your computer. Keylogger Malware (or hardware) that records every keystroke typed, capturing passwords, credit card numbers, and private messages. Lateral Movement The technique used by attackers to progressively move through a network from the initial point of compromise towards high-value targets, using credentials and exploits along the way. Malware Malicious Software — any programme intentionally designed to damage, disrupt, steal from, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system. MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) Authentication requiring two or more verification factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone/token), or something you are (fingerprint/face). Dramatically reduces account compromise risk. MitM (Man-in-the-Middle) An attack where the attacker secretly intercepts and possibly alters communications between two parties, with neither party aware of the interception. OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) Intelligence gathered from publicly available sources: social media, company websites, DNS records, news articles, and public databases. Used in reconnaissance. Passkey A passwordless authentication credential based on FIDO2 standards. Uses public-key cryptography tied to a specific domain, making phishing attacks impossible. Patch A software update that fixes known security vulnerabilities or bugs. Applying patches promptly is one of the most effective defences against cyberattacks. Payload The component of malware that actually causes damage or achieves the attacker's objective — e.g., the encryption module in ransomware or the data-stealing module in spyware. Phishing Deceptive communications (usually email) that impersonate trusted entities to trick recipients into revealing credentials, clicking malicious links, or installing malware. Privilege Escalation Gaining higher permissions than originally granted — typically from standard user to administrator/root — to achieve deeper system control. Ransomware Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment (usually cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. Rootkit Malware designed to hide itself and other malicious software from the OS, antivirus, and administrators — typically by operating at kernel level. SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) A platform that collects, aggregates, and correlates log data from across an organisation's IT infrastructure to detect threats and support incident response. SMB (Server Message Block) A network file-sharing protocol used by Windows. Vulnerabilities in SMB (like EternalBlue) have been exploited by WannaCry and other worms. Social Engineering Psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or revealing confidential information, bypassing technical security controls by targeting human behaviour. Spear Phishing Targeted phishing aimed at a specific individual, using personalised information to increase credibility and success rate. SQL Injection (SQLi) Inserting malicious SQL code into an application input field to manipulate the backend database: extracting, modifying, or deleting data. SSL / TLS Cryptographic protocols that provide encrypted, authenticated communication over the internet. TLS is the modern successor to SSL. HTTPS uses TLS. Supply Chain Attack Compromising a trusted vendor, software provider, or hardware manufacturer to reach their customers — distributing malware through legitimate update channels. Trojan Malware disguised as legitimate, useful software. Relies on user deception to get installed rather than self-propagation. VPN (Virtual Private Network) Creates an encrypted tunnel for internet traffic, hiding content from network observers and masking the user's real IP address. Essential on public Wi-Fi. Vulnerability A weakness or flaw in software, hardware, or configuration that can be exploited by an attacker to compromise security. WAF (Web Application Firewall) A security layer that monitors, filters, and blocks HTTP traffic to and from a web application, protecting against SQLi, XSS, and other web attacks. WPA2 / WPA3 Wi-Fi security protocols. WPA2 is the current standard but has known weaknesses. WPA3 is the newer, more secure successor with improved authentication and encryption. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) Injecting malicious JavaScript into a web page that executes in other users' browsers, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, or page manipulation. Zero-Day A vulnerability that is unknown to the software vendor and therefore has no available patch. Extremely valuable to attackers because no defence exists until it's discovered and fixed. Zero Trust A security model based on "never trust, always verify." No user, device, or system is trusted by default — all access must be continuously authenticated and authorised.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Insider Threats and Supply-Chain Attacks
docs.text:
Not every attack comes from a stranger outside. Some of the most damaging breaches start with an employee, a contractor or a trusted software supplier. This chapter covers three kinds of insider threat (malicious, negligent and compromised) and four kinds of supply-chain attack (software, hardware, open source and third-party). Both families are hard to detect because everything looks authorised.

Layman analogy

Insider threat: hiring a contractor to renovate your house, only to discover they've made copies of all your keys, photographed your valuables, and sold the information to a third party.

Layman analogy

Supply chain attack: trusting a reputable pharmacy to fill your prescription accurately, not realising a compromised employee at the pharmaceutical manufacturer has already adulterated the medication at the source — you trust the brand implicitly and never question it.

docs.title: 11.1 Malicious Insider
docs.text:
An employee, contractor, or partner who intentionally steals data, sabotages systems, leaks sensitive information, or aids external attackers. Often motivated by financial gain, ideology, competitor offers, or resentment (particularly when leaving the organisation).

Example 11.1: Malicious Insider

Edward Snowden (2013): NSA contractor who copied 1.7 million classified US intelligence documents and leaked them to journalists, exposing mass surveillance programmes operated by the NSA and allied agencies. Regardless of the moral debate, this is the textbook definition of a malicious insider with catastrophic, global consequences.

docs.title: 11.2 Negligent Insider
docs.text:
No malicious intent — but careless, uninformed, or hasty actions cause significant data breaches. This includes falling for phishing attacks, misconfiguring cloud storage, using weak passwords, or accidentally emailing sensitive data to the wrong recipient.

Example 11.2: Negligent Insider

2021: A UK university employee accidentally emailed a spreadsheet containing the personal details of 300 students (names, addresses, health information) to the entire student body — a simple but devastating "fat-finger" email error.

docs.title: 11.3 Compromised Insider
docs.text:
A legitimate employee's credentials are stolen by an external attacker, who then uses them to blend in as a trusted insider. This is particularly dangerous because all activity appears to come from a known, trusted employee.

Example 11.3: Compromised Insider

SolarWinds (2020): Attackers used stolen, valid administrator credentials to move through victim networks, appearing to all security monitoring systems as legitimate, authorised administrators conducting routine work.

Detection challenge: All three insider threat types appear as legitimate, authorised users in system logs. Insider threats are among the most difficult attacks to detect and are often discovered months or years after the fact.

docs.title: 11.4 Software Supply Chain Attack
docs.text:
Compromise the software vendor's systems or build process to insert malware into an otherwise legitimate software product. The malware is then distributed to all customers through trusted, digitally signed software updates.

Why it's devastating: Victims voluntarily install the malware themselves. The software is from a trusted, reputable vendor. It is digitally signed. It passes all security scans. There is no suspicious link to click.

Example 11.4: Software Supply Chain Attack

SolarWinds Orion (2020): Attackers attributed to Russian SVR intelligence compromised SolarWinds' build system and inserted the "SUNBURST" backdoor into updates for the Orion IT monitoring platform. 18,000 organisations — including the US Treasury, State Department, Department of Energy, Microsoft, and FireEye — installed the backdoored update. Attackers maintained undetected access for 9 months.

docs.title: 11.5 Hardware Implants
docs.text:
Malicious chips or firmware inserted into hardware components during manufacturing or at some point in the supply chain. Survives complete software reinstallation. Extremely difficult to detect without specialised hardware analysis.

Example 11.5: Hardware Implants

Bloomberg Businessweek (2018) reported that Chinese spy chips were allegedly implanted in Supermicro server motherboards during manufacturing, found in servers used by Apple, Amazon Web Services, and multiple US government contractors. (The companies named disputed the report, but the incident sparked major government review of hardware supply chains.)

docs.title: 11.6 Open Source Poisoning
docs.text:
Inject malicious code into widely used open-source libraries or packages that thousands of other software projects depend on as building blocks.

Example 11.6: Open Source Poisoning

event-stream npm package (2018): A bad actor gained maintainership of this popular JavaScript package (fetched about 2 million times per week). They added a malicious dependency containing code specifically designed to steal Bitcoin wallet credentials from the Copay cryptocurrency app. The malicious code was distributed for weeks before discovery.

docs.title: 11.7 Third-Party Breach (Vendor Pivot)
docs.text:
Attack a smaller, less secure vendor that has legitimate network access to a larger, better-defended target organisation. Use the vendor's credentials and access as a pivot point to reach the primary target.

Example 11.7: Third-Party Breach (Vendor Pivot)

Target Data Breach (2013): Attackers compromised Fazio Mechanical Services — Target's HVAC (heating/ventilation/air conditioning) maintenance vendor. Using Fazio's remote monitoring credentials, attackers pivoted through the vendor access to Target's payment network and installed card-skimming malware on point-of-sale terminals. 40 million credit and debit card numbers were stolen. The breach was traced to an HVAC contractor.

docs.title: 11.8 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Apply least privilege rigorously — employees should only have access to what they specifically need for their role
  • Deploy User and Entity Behaviour Analytics (UEBA) to detect anomalous access patterns
  • Audit and tightly restrict all third-party vendor access — monitor it continuously
  • Require vendors to provide software integrity checksums; verify them before deploying updates
  • Maintain a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) listing all software dependencies and their versions
  • Revoke ALL employee access immediately on their last day of employment — not the following week
  • Conduct thorough background checks for roles with privileged access
  • Implement Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools to detect and alert on unusual data exfiltration

docs.title: 11.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Insiders are malicious, negligent or compromised; all three look like authorised users in logs.
  • Supply-chain attacks target software vendors, hardware, open-source dependencies and third-party vendors, so victims install the attack themselves.
  • SolarWinds (2020) reached 18,000 organisations through a signed update; Target (2013) was breached through an HVAC contractor.
  • Defences: least privilege, behaviour analytics, vendor access control, checksums, SBOMs, prompt de-provisioning and data loss prevention.

docs.title: 11.10 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Classify each as malicious, negligent or compromised insider: (a) an engineer copies the customer database before resigning to join a competitor, (b) an employee emails a spreadsheet of 300 students to the wrong list, (c) an attacker logs in to the VPN with a stolen administrator password.

    Answer

    (a) Malicious. (b) Negligent. (c) Compromised.

  2. Why are insider threats among the hardest attacks to detect?

    Answer

    All three types appear in logs as legitimate, authorised users doing things they are permitted to do, so the usual indicators of an outsider are missing. They are often found months or years later.

  3. Why did the SolarWinds backdoor pass the victims' security checks?

    Answer

    The malicious code was inserted into the vendor's own build process, so the update came from a trusted vendor, was digitally signed and passed all scans. There was no suspicious link to click, and victims installed the update themselves.

  4. What is a Software Bill of Materials and why does it help?

    Answer

    An SBOM lists every component and dependency of a piece of software with its version. When a vulnerable or poisoned library is discovered (as with event-stream), an organisation can immediately tell which of its products contain it.

  5. What lessons does the Target breach teach about third-party access?

    Answer

    A small vendor with network access (an HVAC contractor) was used as a pivot point to reach the payment systems. Vendor access should be limited to the minimum, segmented from sensitive systems and monitored continuously.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Malware
docs.text:
Malware, or malicious software, is any program designed to damage, steal or gain unauthorised access. The many kinds are distinguished by how they spread, how they hide and what damage they do. This chapter works through ten kinds, from the virus, which needs a person to run it, to fileless malware, which never touches the disk. A table at the end of the chapter compares them side by side.

Layman analogy

Just as the biological world has viruses, worms, parasites, bacteria, and toxins — each with different infection strategies and effects on the human body — computer malware comes in distinct "species," each with different strategies and damage profiles.

docs.title: 5.1 Virus
docs.text:
Malicious code that attaches itself to a legitimate file or program. A virus cannot spread on its own — it requires a human action (opening an infected file, running an infected program) to activate and propagate.

Layman analogy

Like a biological virus: it needs a host cell (legitimate file) to exist, and needs you to "touch" it (open the file) to spread to other hosts.

  • Attaches to executables, documents (macro viruses), or boot sectors
  • Requires human action to propagate: opening email attachment, running infected programme
  • Damage: corrupts or deletes files, overwrites boot sector, destroys data

Example 5.1: Virus

ILOVEYOU virus (2000): Arrived as an email with subject "I Love You" and attachment "LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.txt.vbs." When opened, it overwrote image files, music files, and documents, then emailed itself to every contact in the victim's Outlook address book. It spread to 50 million computers in 10 days and caused an estimated $10 billion in damage globally.

docs.title: 5.2 Worm
docs.text:
Self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across networks WITHOUT any user action required. Unlike viruses, worms don't need to attach to a host file — they travel independently.

Layman analogy

A biological worm that reproduces on its own and burrows through soil independently. It doesn't need to attach to a host to exist or spread.

  • Exploits network vulnerabilities to propagate automatically — no human click required
  • Consumes network bandwidth and system resources
  • Often drops additional malware payloads, enables backdoors, or forms botnets

Example 5.2: Worm

WannaCry (2017): Exploited the NSA's "EternalBlue" exploit (stolen from the NSA and leaked online) to attack Windows SMB protocol. Self-propagated across 150 countries in hours. Hit the UK's NHS (forcing cancellation of thousands of medical appointments), Spain's Telefónica, and FedEx. Estimated $4 billion in total damages.

docs.title: 5.3 Trojan Horse
docs.text:
Malware disguised as legitimate, useful software. Unlike viruses, Trojans don't self-replicate — they rely entirely on user deception to get installed.

Layman analogy

The ancient Greek myth: soldiers hide inside a giant wooden horse presented as a gift. Once the Trojans accept the "gift" inside their city walls, the soldiers emerge and attack from within. On your computer: you accept the "gift" (install the software), and the hidden malware attacks from the inside.

  • Disguised as games, utilities, cracked software, fake "security tools," or free applications
  • Once installed: creates backdoors, steals credentials, fetches more malware, grants remote access

Example 5.3: Trojan Horse

Zeus Trojan (2007–present): Disguised as various legitimate software, Zeus infected 3.6 million Windows PCs and stole banking credentials through keylogging and form-grabbing. Used to steal over $70 million from US bank accounts before its source code was leaked in 2011. Its code has since spawned dozens of banking malware variants still active today.

docs.title: 5.4 Ransomware
docs.text:
Encrypts all the victim's files using strong cryptography, then demands a ransom payment (almost always in cryptocurrency, which is harder to trace) for the decryption key. Modern ransomware often also steals data first and threatens to publish it (double extortion).

Layman analogy

Someone breaks into your house, puts industrial padlocks on every single door, drawer, wardrobe, and cabinet, then leaves a note: "Pay $10,000 in Bitcoin to this address for the master key." Even a skilled locksmith (IT expert) cannot open cryptographic locks without the key.

  • Spread via phishing emails with malicious attachments
  • Exploit kits targeting unpatched systems
  • RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) brute-force attacks
  • Supply chain attacks

Example 5.4: Ransomware

Colonial Pipeline (2021): DarkSide ransomware encrypted systems of the largest US fuel pipeline operator. The company paid $4.4 million in Bitcoin ransom and shut down operations for 6 days, causing fuel shortages, panic buying, and a state of emergency across the US East Coast.

docs.title: 5.5 Spyware
docs.text:
Malware that silently monitors all user activity — collecting browsing habits, screenshots, keystrokes, microphone audio, and webcam feeds — and secretly transmits this data to a remote attacker.

Layman analogy

A hidden camera, microphone, and keylogger installed throughout your home, recording everything you do and transmitting a live feed to a complete stranger.

Example 5.5: Spyware

Pegasus spyware (NSO Group): Sold exclusively to governments, used to surveil journalists, human rights activists, lawyers, and political opponents. Could silently activate iPhone and Android microphones and cameras without any user interaction. Exposed in 2021 by Citizen Lab and Amnesty International; found on phones in 50+ countries including those of heads of state.

docs.title: 5.6 Keylogger
docs.text:
Records every keystroke a user types on their keyboard, capturing passwords, credit card numbers, private messages, PINs, and any other information typed.

  • Software keyloggers — malware installed on the system
  • Hardware keyloggers — physical device plugged between the keyboard and the computer (invisible in software scans)
  • Acoustic keyloggers — analyse the sound of keystrokes to reconstruct what was typed

Example 5.6: Keylogger

Olympic Vision keylogger: Targeted business executives across 18 countries via spear-phishing emails, stealing banking credentials and wire transfer authorisations. Used to conduct fraudulent wire transfers from corporate accounts.

docs.title: 5.7 Adware
docs.text:
Automatically displays intrusive advertisements, hijacks browser settings (home page, search engine, new tab page), slows system performance, and may silently install additional malware in the background.

Example 5.7: Adware

Fireball (2017): Discovered by Check Point, this adware infected 250 million PCs worldwide. It hijacked browsers and turned them into automated advertising click-fraud machines, generating revenue for its operators. It also had the full capability to fetch and execute any code from its command server — essentially a backdoor with a monetisation scheme.

docs.title: 5.8 Botnet
docs.text:
A network of malware-infected computers ("bots" or "zombies") all controlled by a central Command-and-Control (C2) server. Infected machine owners typically have no idea their computers are part of the botnet.

Layman analogy

Imagine thousands of people who have been secretly hypnotised. They go about their normal days, but at a signal from the hypnotist, they all simultaneously stop what they're doing and carry out his instructions. The hypnotist (attacker) controls an army without the "soldiers" knowing.

Common botnet uses:

  • DDoS attacks — flood targets with traffic from thousands of sources
  • Spam campaigns — send millions of phishing emails
  • Cryptocurrency mining — use victims' CPU/GPU power to mine crypto for the attacker
  • Credential stuffing — test stolen username/password pairs against services

Example 5.8: Botnet

Mirai Botnet (2016): Infected 600,000 IoT devices (security cameras, home routers, DVRs) by exploiting default, unchanged passwords. Launched the then-largest DDoS attack ever at 1.2 Tbps against Dyn DNS, taking down Twitter, Spotify, Netflix, Reddit, and many other major services for millions of users.

docs.title: 5.9 Logic Bomb
docs.text:
Malicious code hidden inside an otherwise legitimate programme that remains dormant and activates only when a specific condition is met: a particular date, a specific event, a flag being set, or a trigger action.

Layman analogy

A time bomb hidden inside a building's heating system. It sits there doing nothing for months. On a specific date, or when the temperature reaches a specific value, it detonates.

Example 5.9: Logic Bomb

Stuxnet (2010): Reportedly contained logic that acted only on a very specific target configuration, the controllers of Iranian enrichment centrifuges. This precision meant that systems at other facilities appeared to operate normally.

docs.title: 5.10 Fileless Malware
docs.text:
Lives entirely in the computer's RAM memory or Windows registry — never writing a file to disk. Traditional antivirus software scans files on disk; fileless malware never creates any files, making it nearly completely invisible to file-based detection.

Layman analogy

A master thief who enters your home and completes the entire burglary without leaving a single fingerprint, footprint, or physical trace — because they never touch any solid surface and leave before anyone can see them.

docs.title: 5.11 Malware at a glance
docs.text:
The ten kinds of malware can be compared on how they spread and what they do.

Type How it spreads or arrives Typical damage Example from the chapter Virus Attaches to a file; needs a person to run it Corrupts or deletes files, overwrites the boot sector ILOVEYOU (2000) Worm Self-replicates across networks, no user action Consumes bandwidth, drops payloads, opens backdoors WannaCry (2017) Trojan Disguised as useful software; the user installs it Backdoors, data theft, fetches more malware Zeus Ransomware Phishing, exploit kits, RDP brute force, supply chain Encrypts files, demands cryptocurrency Colonial Pipeline (2021) Spyware Bundled software, browser extensions, phishing Silently collects browsing, keystrokes, screenshots, camera Pegasus Keylogger Malware, a hardware device or phishing Records every keystroke Olympic Vision Adware Free-software installers, fake browser updates Intrusive ads, hijacked browser, may install more malware Fireball (2017) Botnet Exploit kits, phishing or other malware DDoS, spam, mining, credential stuffing Mirai (2016) Logic bomb Inserted by insiders or other malware Destructive payload at a set time or condition Stuxnet Fileless malware Memory and registry only, nothing on disk Evades file-based antivirus (no single example named)

docs.title: 5.12 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Use up-to-date antivirus/antimalware with real-time protection — but know it's not a silver bullet
  • NEVER open unexpected email attachments or enable macros in Office documents from unknown senders
  • Maintain regular, tested offline backups — the only true defence against ransomware is a clean backup
  • Change ALL default passwords on every device, especially smart home (IoT) devices
  • Use Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) for behavioural monitoring that catches fileless malware
  • Use application whitelisting to prevent unauthorised software from executing

docs.title: 5.13 Summary
docs.text:
• Malware types differ in how they spread (virus needs a person; worm needs no one; trojan relies on deception), how they hide (rootkit, fileless) and what they do (ransomware, spyware, keylogger, adware, botnet).
  • Ransomware often steals data first (double extortion), so a clean offline backup is necessary but not always sufficient.
  • A botnet is a network of infected machines under one command-and-control server; Mirai built one from default-password IoT devices.
  • No single defence works: combine updated antivirus, EDR, whitelisting, tested offline backups and the removal of default passwords.

docs.title: 5.14 Exercises
docs.text:
1. State how a virus, a worm and a trojan each spread.

    Answer

    A virus attaches to a legitimate file and needs a person to run it. A worm replicates itself across networks without any user action. A trojan is disguised as useful software and relies on the user installing it; it does not self-replicate.

  2. Why does double extortion mean that backups alone do not defeat modern ransomware?

    Answer

    The attacker steals the data before encrypting it and threatens to publish it. A backup lets you restore your files but does nothing about the leak, so you still face the threat of exposure.

  3. Why does fileless malware evade traditional antivirus, and what detects it?

    Answer

    It lives in RAM or the registry and never writes a file to disk, whereas traditional antivirus scans files. Endpoint detection and response watches behaviour, such as unusual use of system tools, and can catch it.

  4. List four uses of a botnet and say how Mirai recruited its bots.

    Answer

    DDoS attacks, spam and phishing campaigns, cryptocurrency mining and credential stuffing. Mirai recruited about 600,000 IoT devices (cameras, routers, DVRs) by trying default, unchanged passwords.

  5. Classify each as virus, worm, trojan, botnet or ransomware: WannaCry, Zeus, Mirai, DarkSide at Colonial Pipeline.

    Answer

    WannaCry: worm (it spread through the SMB flaw EternalBlue with no user action). Zeus: trojan (banking credentials stolen by software disguised as legitimate). Mirai: botnet. DarkSide at Colonial Pipeline: ransomware.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Network Attacks
docs.text:
Network attacks target the roads of the internet: the protocols, the devices and the traffic that carry data between computers. They exploit the fact that many core protocols were designed when every participant could be trusted. This chapter covers interception (man-in-the-middle, sniffing), forgery (IP spoofing, DNS spoofing, replay) and flooding (DoS and DDoS), and shows how a few simple ideas, such as pretending to be someone else's address, underlie them all.

Layman analogy

Think of the internet as a global postal system. Network attacks are like intercepting mail, forging return addresses, flooding the sorting office with fake letters, or redirecting parcels to the wrong destination.

docs.title: 2.1 Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attack
docs.text: The attacker secretly inserts themselves between two communicating parties, intercepting — and potentially altering — all communications without either party realising.

docs.title: ARP Poisoning
docs.text:
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to physical hardware (MAC) addresses on a local network. The attacker sends fake ARP messages, poisoning devices into sending traffic to the attacker's machine instead of the intended recipient.

Layman analogy

Forging name labels on every mailbox in an apartment building so that your neighbours' post is delivered to your door instead.

docs.title: SSL Stripping
docs.text:
The attacker intercepts the connection between a user and a website, downgrading a secure HTTPS connection to an unencrypted HTTP connection. The user thinks they are on a secure site; the attacker can read everything.

Layman analogy

Converting a sealed, tamper-proof courier envelope into an open postcard that anyone can read as it travels through the postal system.

docs.title: BGP Hijacking
docs.text:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing system of the internet. Attackers announce false routes, redirecting internet traffic through their infrastructure before passing it to the legitimate destination.

Layman analogy

Changing motorway exit signs so that traffic heading to London gets routed through a different town where it can be monitored or tampered with, before eventually arriving at the correct destination.

Example 2.1: BGP Hijacking

In 2010, China Telecom advertised routes for 15% of the world's internet traffic through Chinese servers, rerouting data from governments, military networks, and large corporations for 18 minutes.

Figure 2.1. ARP poisoning: forged ARP replies make the victim send its traffic to the attacker, who forwards it on to the gateway, reading and possibly changing it.

docs.title: 2.2 DoS and DDoS Attacks
docs.text:
A Denial of Service (DoS) attack uses a single source to overwhelm a target. A Distributed DoS (DDoS) attack uses thousands or millions of compromised computers (a botnet) simultaneously, making it nearly impossible to block.

Layman analogy

DoS is one person blocking a shop doorway. DDoS is 10,000 people simultaneously blocking every entrance, exit, and window of the building.

Volume-Based Attacks: Saturate bandwidth with massive traffic.

  • UDP Flood — spoof source IP and flood all ports with UDP packets
  • ICMP Flood — overwhelm target with ping requests
  • DNS Amplification — small request generates 50x larger response sent to victim
  • NTP Amplification — uses time servers that respond up to 556x the request size

Protocol-Based Attacks: Exhaust server or network equipment resources.

  • SYN Flood — exploit TCP handshake; server stores half-open connections until memory is exhausted
  • Ping of Death — malformed oversized packets crash systems on reassembly
  • Smurf Attack — broadcast ICMP with spoofed victim IP; entire network replies to victim

Application Layer Attacks: Target specific services with lower traffic volumes — harder to detect.

  • HTTP Flood — legitimate-looking requests overwhelm web server
  • Slowloris — thousands of slow, partial connections exhaust the server's connection limit
  • RUDY (R-U-Dead-Yet) — extremely slow POST bodies tie up server threads indefinitely

Example 2.2: DoS and DDoS Attacks

  • 2016: Mirai botnet hit Dyn DNS at 1.2 Tbps — took down Twitter, Netflix, Reddit.
  • 2018: GitHub survived 1.35 Tbps memcached amplification.
  • 2020: AWS Shield stopped 2.3 Tbps — the largest DDoS recorded at that time.
  • 2022: Google blocked 46 million requests/second HTTPS flood from thousands of sources.
Figure 2.2. A normal TCP handshake completes with an ACK; in a SYN flood the final ACK never arrives, and half-open entries fill the server's connection table. Figure 2.3. DNS amplification: a small query with the victim's address as its source produces a much larger response, which the resolver sends to the victim.

Example 2.2b: the arithmetic of amplification

A botnet sends 20 Mbit/s of spoofed DNS queries. Each response is up to 50 times larger than the query, so the traffic aimed at the victim is \(20\times50=1000\) Mbit/s, which is 1 Gbit/s. The attacker pays for 20 Mbit/s and the victim receives fifty times more. This is why amplification attacks are favoured, and why filtering spoofed source addresses (BCP38) matters: if the forged query never leaves the attacker's network, there is nothing to amplify.

docs.title: 2.3 Packet Sniffing
docs.text:
Capturing raw network packets as they travel through the network. On unencrypted networks, packet contents are fully readable.

  • Active Sniffing — ARP/MAC flooding to capture traffic on switched networks
  • Passive Sniffing — simply listening on hub-based networks (no interference needed)
  • Promiscuous Mode — configuring a network card to capture ALL traffic, not just traffic addressed to it

Example 2.3: Packet Sniffing

On an unencrypted public Wi-Fi network, any attacker running Wireshark can see every website you visit, every form you submit, and every cookie your browser sends — including login session tokens.

docs.title: 2.4 DNS Spoofing / Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's "phone book" — it translates domain names (google.com) into IP addresses. An attacker corrupts DNS records to redirect legitimate lookups to malicious servers.

Layman analogy

Someone has tampered with the phone book so that when you look up your bank's phone number, you get the attacker's number instead. You call it thinking it's your bank.

  • Cache Poisoning — inject false DNS records into a resolver's cache
  • DNS Hijacking via Router — change router DNS settings to attacker-controlled servers
  • Authoritative Server Compromise — hack the actual DNS authority for a domain

docs.title: 2.5 IP Spoofing
docs.text:
Forging the source IP address in network packets to impersonate another host or bypass IP-based security filters.

Layman analogy

Sending a letter with someone else's return address. The recipient thinks the letter came from the faked address and may act accordingly.

  • Used in DDoS amplification — send requests with victim's IP so amplified responses flood the victim
  • Blind spoofing — no response needed; used for one-way attacks
  • Non-blind spoofing — attacker is on the same subnet and can observe responses

docs.title: 2.6 Replay Attack
docs.text:
The attacker captures a valid authentication token or data packet and retransmits it later to gain unauthorised access, without ever cracking the password.

Layman analogy

Recording the exact beep sequence of your garage door opener, then playing the recording back later to open the garage — without knowing the code yourself.

docs.title: 2.7 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Always use HTTPS — look for the padlock icon in your browser address bar
  • Use a VPN (Virtual Private Network) on any public Wi-Fi network
  • Enable DNSSEC on your domains to cryptographically verify DNS responses
  • Use DDoS mitigation services like Cloudflare or AWS Shield for critical services
  • Configure firewalls to block packets with spoofed source IP addresses (BCP38 standard)

docs.title: 2.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Man-in-the-middle attacks insert the attacker into a conversation: ARP poisoning on a local network, SSL stripping to downgrade HTTPS, BGP hijacking to reroute traffic across the internet.
  • Spoofing attacks forge an identity: IP spoofing forges a source address, DNS spoofing corrupts the address book; replay retransmits a captured valid message.
  • DoS and DDoS attacks exhaust bandwidth, server resources or an application, and amplification lets a small request produce a large response aimed at the victim.
  • Defences: HTTPS, VPNs, DNSSEC, DDoS mitigation services and filtering of spoofed source addresses (BCP38).

docs.title: 2.9 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Describe ARP poisoning in two sentences. Why does it work only on a local network?

    Answer

    ARP maps IP addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses on a local network. The attacker sends forged ARP messages that make other devices believe the attacker's MAC address belongs to the gateway (or another host), so their traffic flows through the attacker. ARP operates only within one local network segment, so the attacker must be on it.

  2. A botnet sends 40 Mbit/s of spoofed DNS queries to open resolvers whose responses are 50 times larger than the queries. What traffic reaches the victim?

    Answer

    \(40\times50=2000\) Mbit/s, or 2 Gbit/s. The attacker spends 40 Mbit/s and the victim receives fifty times as much, which is why amplification is attractive.

  3. Explain how a SYN flood exhausts a server, and how SYN cookies defend against it.

    Answer

    The attacker sends many SYN packets and never completes the handshake with the final ACK. The server allocates memory for each half-open connection and waits until its table is full. SYN cookies encode the needed state in the sequence number of the SYN-ACK, so the server stores nothing until a valid ACK returns.

  4. Distinguish blind from non-blind IP spoofing.

    Answer

    In blind spoofing the attacker forges the source address and cannot see replies, so it suits one-way attacks such as floods. In non-blind spoofing the attacker is on the same subnet and can observe the responses, so it can take part in a two-way exchange.

  5. A user visits a site that normally uses HTTPS but the browser shows plain HTTP after an attacker on the network intervened. Which attack is this, and why is "always use HTTPS" not a complete answer?

    Answer

    This is SSL stripping: the attacker downgrades the connection to HTTP. The user must still notice the missing padlock. Sites can prevent the downgrade by telling browsers to use HTTPS only (HTTP Strict Transport Security), and a VPN protects traffic on untrusted networks.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Password Attacks
docs.text:
Passwords remain the most commonly attacked authentication mechanism. The attacks range from brute force, which tries everything, to credential phishing, which needs no cracking at all because the victim simply types the password into the wrong page. This chapter covers six attacks, shows the arithmetic that makes brute force practical against short passwords, and explains why salting, multi-factor authentication and passkeys defeat so many of them.

Layman analogy

If a password is the key to a lock: brute force is trying every possible key in a massive ring of millions of keys; a dictionary attack is trying the most commonly cut keys first; credential stuffing is using a copy of someone else's key; and credential phishing is tricking you into handing the attacker your own key directly.

docs.title: 9.1 Brute Force Attack
docs.text:
Systematically try every possible combination of characters until the correct password is found. Given enough time and computing power, brute force can crack any password.

Layman analogy

Trying every possible combination on a padlock — 0000, 0001, 0002... all the way to 9999. On a 4-digit lock this takes up to 10,000 attempts. On an 8-character password with letters, numbers, and symbols, it takes trillions.

The mathematics:

  • 8-character lowercase password: 26⁸ = 208 billion combinations
  • Modern GPUs: ~100 billion hash calculations per second
  • Result: an 8-character all-lowercase password is cracked in approximately 2 seconds
  • 12-character mixed password: would take thousands of years at the same rate

Defence tip

Use long passwords (15+ characters). Enable account lockout policies and rate limiting. Enable MFA.

docs.title: 9.2 Dictionary Attack
docs.text:
Instead of trying every possible combination, try a pre-compiled list of common words, phrases, number sequences, and known passwords from previous breaches.

Key fact: The RockYou.txt wordlist — compiled from a 2009 data breach — contains 14 million real passwords people actually use. Research shows 80%+ of users have a password that appears somewhere in common wordlists.

Layman analogy

Instead of trying every combination on a combination lock, an attacker who knows that most people use "1234," "0000," or their birth year tries those first. This is dramatically faster and more effective than exhaustive search.

Defence tip

Never use real dictionary words, names, or dates. Use a passphrase: "Tr@in$RainFall!2024" or a random password manager-generated string.

docs.title: 9.3 Rainbow Table Attack
docs.text:
Websites store passwords as cryptographic hashes (a one-way mathematical transformation) — not the plain text. When attackers steal a password database, they get hashes and need to reverse them. A rainbow table is a pre-computed database of hash→password mappings, allowing instant lookup.

  • Rainbow table for 8-character alphanumeric MD5 passwords: ~460 GB storage
  • Lookup time: milliseconds (vs. hours or days for live brute force)

Layman analogy

Instead of solving a maths problem every time you need the answer, you pre-compute and store every possible answer in a giant lookup table. Finding the answer becomes trivial — just look it up.

Defence tip
