Password SALTING: Before hashing, add a unique random string ("salt") to each password. Even if two users have the same password, their hashes will be completely different. This makes pre-computed rainbow tables entirely useless.

docs.title: 9.4 Credential Stuffing
docs.text:
Use username/password pairs stolen from one breached service to attempt login on completely different services, exploiting the widespread habit of password reuse.

Why it works: Studies consistently show that 65% of people reuse the same password across multiple accounts.

Scale: leaked-credential collections such as the "Compilation of Many Breaches" (COMB) hold billions of username and password pairs harvested from many breaches over many years.

Example 9.4: Credential Stuffing

The 2018 MyFitnessPal breach exposed about 150 million accounts. Wherever users had reused the same email address and password on other services, the leaked pair could be tried against those accounts, which is exactly how credential stuffing works.

Defence tip

Use a unique, strong password for EVERY service. A password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, Dashlane) makes this practical. Enable MFA everywhere.

docs.title: 9.5 Password Spraying
docs.text:
The inverse of brute force. Instead of trying MANY passwords against ONE account (which triggers lockouts), try ONE or a very few common passwords against THOUSANDS of accounts. Stays under lockout thresholds while compromising accounts at scale.

Example: Try the single password "Summer2024!" against 10,000 accounts. With a 3-5% success rate (typical for common passwords), the attacker compromises 300-500 accounts without triggering any individual account lockout.

Defence tip

MFA eliminates the value of spraying even when passwords are correctly guessed. Implement anomaly detection for distributed authentication attempts.

docs.title: 9.6 Credential Phishing
docs.text:
Trick users into voluntarily typing their real credentials into a fake login page. No cracking required — the attacker simply receives whatever the victim types.

  • Modlishka — real-time reverse proxy that shows the actual legitimate website to the victim but intercepts all input, including MFA tokens, relaying them in real time
  • Gophish — open-source phishing campaign platform

Defence tip

FIDO2 / Passkeys: Phishing-resistant by design. Authentication is cryptographically bound to the specific domain — a fake site can never trigger the authenticator, even if the victim is fooled.

docs.title: 9.7 Brute force in numbers
docs.text:
Figure 9.1. Time to try every combination at $10^{11}$ guesses per second, against password length, for three character sets. Each extra character multiplies the work by the size of the set.

Example 9.7: how long does a brute-force search take?

The number of passwords of length \(n\) over an alphabet of size \(s\) is \(s^n\).

  • 8 lowercase letters: \(26^8=208{,}827{,}064{,}576\approx2.1\times10^{11}\). At \(10^{11}\) guesses per second this takes about 2 seconds.
  • 12 characters from the 94 printable characters: \(94^{12}\approx4.8\times10^{23}\). At the same rate this takes about \(4.8\times10^{12}\) seconds, roughly 150,000 years.

Adding four characters and widening the alphabet multiplied the work by a factor of about \(2\times10^{12}\). Length is the cheapest defence, and the reason the chapter advises passwords of 15 or more characters. The rate itself is the figure quoted in the course material for modern GPUs against fast hashes; slow, salted password hashes reduce it dramatically, which is why how a service stores passwords matters as much as what users choose.

docs.title: 9.8 Tools and defences at a glance
docs.text:
The tools below are named in the security literature and are also used by defenders to test their own systems.

Attack Tools seen in the literature Typical defence Brute force Hashcat, John the Ripper, Hydra Long passwords, lockout policies, rate limiting Dictionary Hashcat with wordlists, CrackStation, CUPP Avoid real words; use passphrases Rainbow table RainbowCrack Salting Credential stuffing Sentry MBA, OpenBullet, custom scripts A unique password per site, MFA Password spraying Ruler (Exchange), Spray, MSOLSpray (Azure) MFA, anomaly detection, conditional access Credential phishing Gophish, Modlishka FIDO2 passkeys

docs.title: 9.9 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Use a password manager — generate and store a unique, random password for every service
  • Enable MFA on every account, especially email (which controls account recovery for everything else) and banking
  • Check your exposure at HaveIBeenPwned.com — if your email appears, change that password everywhere
  • Consider Passkeys (FIDO2) — they fundamentally cannot be phished or credential-stuffed
  • Organisations: implement password spray detection, anomaly alerts, and conditional access policies

docs.title: 9.10 Summary
docs.text:
• Brute force tries every combination; dictionary attacks try likely passwords; rainbow tables look up precomputed hashes; credential stuffing reuses leaked pairs; spraying tries few passwords on many accounts; credential phishing needs no cracking.
  • Length beats complexity: an 8-character lowercase password falls in about 2 seconds at \(10^{11}\) guesses per second.
  • Salting defeats rainbow tables; a unique password per site and MFA defeat stuffing and spraying; passkeys (FIDO2) defeat phishing.
  • Use a password manager and check exposure at Have I Been Pwned.

docs.title: 9.11 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compute the number of 8-character lowercase passwords and how long it takes to try them all at \(10^{11}\) guesses per second.

    Answer

    \(26^8=208{,}827{,}064{,}576\approx2.1\times10^{11}\). At \(10^{11}\) guesses per second, that is about 2.1 seconds.

  2. How does password spraying differ from brute force, and why does it avoid lockouts?

    Answer

    Brute force tries many passwords against one account, which triggers lockout. Spraying tries one or a few very common passwords against thousands of accounts, so no single account sees enough failures to lock. A 3 to 5 percent success rate on 10,000 accounts yields 300 to 500 compromised accounts.

  3. Why does salting make rainbow tables useless? What if two users have the same password?

    Answer

    A rainbow table is precomputed for passwords without salt. With a unique random salt added before hashing, the attacker would need a separate table for every possible salt. Two users with the same password get different hashes.

  4. Why are FIDO2 passkeys phishing-resistant, even if the user is fooled by a fake login page?

    Answer

    The credential is cryptographically bound to the genuine domain. A fake site has a different domain, so the authenticator will not respond to it, and no password or reusable secret is ever typed or transmitted.

  5. List three defences against credential stuffing.

    Answer

    A unique password for every service (practical with a password manager), multi-factor authentication, and checking whether your email appears in known breaches (for example Have I Been Pwned) and changing any reused password. Organisations can also detect anomalous login attempts.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Phishing and Its Variants
docs.text:
Phishing is the use of deceptive messages to trick people into giving up credentials, clicking malicious links or running malware. It is the most common way into an organisation, and it comes in many variants that differ by medium (email, text message, voice, social media), by target (anyone, one person, an executive) and by technique. This chapter covers eight variants.

Layman analogy

Receiving a perfectly convincing fake letter from your bank, printed on what looks like official letterhead, asking you to call a number to "verify your account details for security purposes." The letter looks real; the phone number is not your bank's.

docs.title: 6.1 Email Phishing (Mass Phishing)
docs.text:
Bulk emails sent to thousands or millions of random recipients, impersonating well-known brands: banks, streaming services, online retailers, government agencies.

  • Look-alike domains: "paypa1.com", "netf1ix-support.com", "amazon-security-alert.net"
  • Malicious email attachments: Word documents with macros, PDFs with embedded scripts
  • Spoofed sender addresses that appear legitimate at first glance

Example 6.1: Email Phishing (Mass Phishing)

"Your Netflix account is suspended — verify immediately at netf1ix-support.com." Millions of such emails are sent. Even if only 0.1% of recipients click, that's still thousands of compromised accounts. The economics work for the attacker even with an almost total failure rate.

docs.title: 6.2 Spear Phishing
docs.text:
Highly targeted phishing aimed at a specific named individual, using personalised details gathered through research (LinkedIn, company website, social media, prior data breaches) to make the message appear completely legitimate.

Layman analogy

Instead of a generic "Dear Customer" letter, you receive: "Hi Sarah, following up on the Q3 budget review you discussed with Mark on Tuesday — the updated figures are in the attached document." Specific, plausible, and deeply alarming.

Example 6.2: Spear Phishing

The 2016 DNC Hack: A spear-phishing email was sent specifically to John Podesta (Hillary Clinton's campaign chairman), stating his Google password needed to be urgently changed. The email linked to a convincing fake Google login page. He entered his real credentials. Thousands of campaign emails were subsequently published.

docs.title: 6.3 Whaling
docs.text:
Spear phishing specifically aimed at C-suite executives (CEO, CFO, CISO, CTO) — the highest-value targets with authority to authorise large financial transactions, access the most sensitive data, or override security controls.

Common scenario — Business Email Compromise (CEO Fraud): The attacker spoofs the CEO's email and messages the CFO: "This is confidential and urgent. Wire $2.3M to our acquisition partner's account immediately. Do not discuss with anyone. I'll explain after."

Example 6.3: Whaling

2019 — Toyota Boshoku Corporation: Employees were deceived via whaling/Business Email Compromise into changing wire transfer account details. The company lost $37 million in a single fraudulent transaction.

docs.title: 6.4 Smishing (SMS Phishing)
docs.text:
Phishing attacks conducted via SMS text messages. These are particularly dangerous because text messages bypass email filters and appear in the same inbox as genuine messages from your bank.

Example message: "USPS: Your parcel could not be delivered due to incorrect address. Update your details at usps-parcel-update[.]ru within 24 hours or it will be returned."

Example 6.4: Smishing (SMS Phishing)

During the COVID-19 pandemic, smishing attacks impersonating government health agencies and tax authorities to offer "stimulus payments" or "test results" surged massively, with hundreds of millions of malicious texts sent across the US, UK, and Australia.

docs.title: 6.5 Vishing (Voice Phishing)
docs.text:
Phishing conducted via telephone calls, with attackers impersonating banks, the IRS/HMRC, Microsoft support, police, or other authorities to extract information or money.

Common script: "Hello, this is Microsoft Technical Support. We have detected a critical virus on your computer. I need remote access to remove it immediately before your data is destroyed."

Example 6.5: Vishing (Voice Phishing)

Twitter Hack (2020): A teenager orchestrated a vishing campaign against Twitter employees, calling them and impersonating the IT department. He convinced multiple employees to grant access to internal administrative tools. This allowed compromise of 130 high-profile accounts (Barack Obama, Elon Musk, Apple, Joe Biden) to run a Bitcoin scam that generated $120,000 in 3 hours.

docs.title: 6.6 Pharming
docs.text:
Redirect users from legitimate websites to fake replica sites WITHOUT requiring them to click any malicious link — accomplished by poisoning DNS caches or modifying the local "hosts" file.

Layman analogy

You correctly type "paypal.com" into your browser. But someone has altered the internet's address book (DNS) so that paypal.com now resolves to the attacker's IP address. You see a pixel-perfect replica of PayPal. Everything you type goes to the attacker. You never clicked anything suspicious.

docs.title: 6.7 Angler Phishing
docs.text:
Attackers create fake customer service accounts on social media (Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram) and monitor for users publicly complaining about real companies. They respond to those complaints offering "help" — which is actually credential theft.

Example: User tweets "@Barclays my account is locked, please help!" — Attacker replies from @BarclaysHelpTeam1 (fake account): "We're sorry for the inconvenience! Please DM us your account number and date of birth to verify your identity and unlock your account."

docs.title: 6.8 Clone Phishing
docs.text:
A legitimate, previously delivered email (e.g., a DHL parcel tracking update, a LinkedIn notification) is cloned exactly. The real attachment or link is replaced with a malicious one, and it is resent appearing to be a "follow-up," "correction," or "updated version."

Layman analogy

Someone makes a perfect photocopy of a real letter from your bank, changes the phone number at the bottom to their own, and puts it in your post box. It looks identical to the real thing.

docs.title: 6.9 Phishing variants at a glance
docs.text:
The eight variants differ by medium, target and technique.

Variant Medium Typical target Technique Email phishing Email Mass, sent to thousands at random Fake login pages, attachments, look-alike domains Spear phishing Email One researched individual Personalised with name, employer and colleagues Whaling Email C-suite executives Highly tailored; spoofed board members or lawyers Smishing SMS Any mobile user Link or urgent call to action in a text Vishing Voice call Elderly people, employees, customers Impersonates a bank, tax office, tech support or government Pharming Poisoned DNS or hosts file All web users Redirects a correct address to a fake site Angler phishing Social media Users who complain publicly Fake customer-service account replies Clone phishing Email Previous recipients Copies a real email, swaps the link or attachment

docs.title: 6.10 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Never click links in emails — type the organisation's address directly into your browser
  • Verify unexpected requests by calling the organisation on their OFFICIAL published number — never the number in the email
  • Enable MFA on ALL accounts — even if credentials are stolen, MFA prevents login without the second factor
  • Check for domain name oddities: "paypa1.com" vs "paypal.com", "amazon-alerts.net" vs "amazon.com"
  • Organisations should implement email authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records
  • For wire transfers requested by email: ALWAYS call the requestor on a known number to verbally confirm

docs.title: 6.11 Summary
docs.text:
• Phishing variants differ by medium (email, SMS, voice, social media), target (mass, one person, executives) and technique (look-alike domains, cloned messages, poisoned DNS).
  • Mass phishing works on economics: even if 0.1% of recipients respond, the cost to the attacker is tiny.
  • Pharming needs no click: it poisons DNS or the hosts file so that the correct address leads to a fake site.
  • Defences: verify through an official channel you find yourself, use MFA, check the domain carefully, and have the organisation deploy SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

docs.title: 6.12 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compare email phishing, spear phishing, whaling and clone phishing by target and technique.

    Answer

    Email phishing: mass, sent to thousands, with fake login pages and look-alike domains. Spear phishing: one researched individual, with personal details. Whaling: spear phishing aimed at C-suite executives, often business email compromise. Clone phishing: copies a legitimate email the victim already received and swaps in a malicious link or attachment.

  2. List three signs that "netf1ix-support.com" is not Netflix.

    Answer

    The "i" is replaced by the digit 1; the domain is not netflix.com but a different one with "-support" added; the message demands urgent verification. The domain, not the display name, decides who owns the site.

  3. Why do smishing messages tend to be believed more readily than phishing emails?

    Answer

    Text messages bypass email filters and arrive in the same inbox as genuine messages from the victim's bank or courier, and they are short and urgent.

  4. What is the key difference between phishing and pharming?

    Answer

    Phishing needs the victim to click a deceptive link or open a message. Pharming needs no click: DNS or the hosts file is poisoned so that typing the correct address leads to the fake site.

  5. What do SPF, DKIM and DMARC do?

    Answer

    SPF lists which servers may send mail for a domain. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature that proves the message was sent by the domain and not altered. DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail that fails those checks and reports back. Together they make spoofing the organisation's own domain much harder.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is a beginner's map of the attacks that threaten computers, networks, people and organisations. It is written for first-year students, for professionals in other fields who need to talk to security teams, and for anyone who reads about "a breach" in the news and wants to know what actually happened. No prior technical knowledge is needed. Every attack is explained in plain English, with a layman's analogy, a real incident and the defences that work.

The word taxonomy means a system of classification, and classification is the real subject. Security professionals do not meet attacks one at a time. They meet families: attacks that share a target, a technique or an attacker. Learning the families lets you recognise a new attack you have never seen, because it will almost always be a variant of one you know.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The book follows the order of the original course material, from the broadest classification to the most specialised.

Chapter Topic The question it answers 1 Active and passive attacks Does the attacker change anything? 2 Network attacks How is traffic intercepted, forged or flooded? 3 Web application attacks How do attackers abuse websites and APIs? 4 System and operating-system attacks How is the machine itself taken over? 5 Malware What kinds of malicious software exist? 6 Phishing How do deceptive messages work? 7 Social engineering How is human psychology exploited? 8 Denial of service in depth How are services knocked offline? 9 Password attacks How is authentication broken? 10 Wireless attacks What can an attacker do over the air? 11 Insider threats and supply chains What if the danger is already inside? 12 Advanced persistent threats How do patient nation-state campaigns unfold? 13 Defence principles What ties all the defences together?

An appendix gives a one-page quick-reference table of the main attacks, followed by a glossary and a list of further resources.

docs.title: How each chapter works
docs.text:
Each attack is presented in the same way. A short definition says what the attacker does. A layman analogy (a green box) gives an everyday picture. A real-world example (a box headed "Example") gives a documented incident. A defence tip (a blue box) says what to do about it. Every chapter ends with a checklist of defences, a summary and exercises with folded answers.

Use this knowledge responsibly

The techniques described here are explained so that you can defend against them. Attacking a system, network or person without the owner's permission is a crime in most countries. Practise only on systems that you own or have written authority to test.

A note on the numbers

The incident figures (records stolen, money lost, devices infected) and the survey figures (such as the share of breaches that begin with phishing) are those quoted in the course material. They are the commonly reported numbers, and different sources sometimes give different values. Treat them as indicative, not exact. Where a figure is disputed, the text says so.

docs.title: The main attacks at a glance
docs.text:
This table summarises the main attacks of the book. Difficulty means the skill and resources needed by the attacker: very low is a script kiddie and very high is nation-state level. Impact runs Low, High, Critical.

Attack type Category Attacker goal Primary vector Difficulty Impact SQL injection Web application Database theft or manipulation Web input field Low Critical XSS Web application Session hijacking Web form or URL parameter Low High Phishing Social engineering Credential theft Email or SMS Very low High Spear phishing Social engineering Targeted access Personalised email Medium Critical Ransomware Malware Financial gain Email, RDP or USB Medium Critical DDoS Network Disrupt service Botnet traffic flood Low High Man-in-the-middle Network Intercept data Same network, ARP Medium Critical Brute force Password Account access Authentication endpoint Low High Zero-day System Undetectable access Any unpatched surface Very high Critical APT Advanced Long-term espionage Multiple vectors Very high Critical Supply chain Advanced Mass compromise Vendor or software update High Critical Insider threat Physical and human Sabotage or theft Physical or authorised access Low Critical

docs.title: Chapter 7: Social Engineering
docs.text:
Social engineering attacks the human rather than the machine. Attackers exploit trust in authority, the wish to be helpful, fear, curiosity and social pressure. Because no software patch fixes a person, these attacks succeed even against organisations with strong technical defences. This chapter covers six tactics and the psychological trigger each one pulls.

Layman analogy

Technical hacking is like picking a lock. Social engineering is like convincing the homeowner to hand you the key willingly — while they think they're doing the right thing.

docs.title: 7.1 Pretexting
docs.text:
Creating an elaborate, fabricated scenario (the "pretext") to extract information or manipulate someone into taking a specific action. The attacker builds trust through a plausible cover story.

Example: "Good morning, I'm Dave from the IT Security team. We're rolling out a critical security patch today and need to verify your VPN credentials to ensure compatibility. Could I get your username and current password?"

Defence tip

Real IT departments will NEVER ask for your password — over email, phone, or in person. If someone asks, it is an attack. Always call back on a number you find independently.

docs.title: 7.2 Baiting
docs.text:
Luring victims with something enticing — free software offers, prizes, or physical media like USB drives — to get them to take an action that compromises security.

Famous experiment: A USB drive labelled "PAYROLL CONFIDENTIAL Q4 2024" is left "accidentally" in a company car park. Research studies consistently show that 45–60% of employees who find such drives plug them into company computers — out of curiosity or a sense of duty.

Example 7.2: Baiting

Stuxnet (2010): The malware is widely reported to have reached air-gapped (no internet connection) Iranian nuclear facilities on USB drives, plugged in by people who did not know what they carried. The exact route has never been officially confirmed. If it is right, it shows how a trusted-looking drive can carry an attack into the most secure networks.

Defence tip

Never plug in USB drives found in public places. Disable AutoRun/AutoPlay on all work computers.

docs.title: 7.3 Tailgating / Piggybacking
docs.text:
Physically following an authorised person through a badge-controlled, secure access point without swiping your own credentials. The attack relies on the natural human instinct to be polite and hold doors open.

Example: "Hi, sorry — could you hold that? My hands are completely full of boxes and my badge is in my pocket." The attacker walks straight through a secured entrance without any authentication.

Defence tip

Challenge everyone without a visible, valid badge — every single time. True security means being willing to be briefly impolite. "Politeness costs you your security."

docs.title: 7.4 Quid Pro Quo
docs.text:
The attacker offers something of value — usually a service — in exchange for information or access. The "helpful" act first creates a sense of obligation and trust.

"Hi, I'm from Microsoft IT Services. I can see from our monitoring that your computer is running very slowly. I can fix that for you right now, for free, if you just give me remote access for a few minutes."

The victim thinks: "Great, free IT help!" — but the attacker now has full remote access to install malware, steal data, or establish a persistent backdoor.

Defence tip

Your organisation has its own IT department. Unsolicited technical "help" from strangers is always a red flag. Refuse and report it immediately.

docs.title: 7.5 Urgency / Scarcity Tactics
docs.text:
Creating artificial time pressure that forces a victim to act immediately without taking time to think, question, or verify. Urgency short-circuits rational decision-making.

"CRITICAL ALERT: Your account has been compromised. You must verify your identity within the next 2 hours or your account will be PERMANENTLY and IRREVERSIBLY deleted along with all your data."

Defence tip

PAUSE. Any legitimate organisation will give you adequate time to verify. Artificial urgency is the single most reliable indicator of a social engineering attack. Slow down — verify independently through official channels.

docs.title: 7.6 Consensus / Social Proof
docs.text:
Making an unusual request seem normal and safe by claiming that peers, colleagues, or authority figures have already complied with the same request.

"This is HR. All employees have already submitted their updated login credentials for the new payroll system migration. You're one of the last few remaining. Please send yours by end of business today."

Defence tip

Verify independently by calling HR or IT directly on numbers you find yourself. Real system migrations never require employees to submit their passwords — that's what Single Sign-On (SSO) is for.

docs.title: 7.7 The psychology behind the tactics
docs.text:
Each tactic pulls a particular lever of human behaviour. Seeing the lever is the best protection, because once you can name the pressure you are under, you can step back from it.

Tactic Main psychological trigger Pretexting Authority and trust Baiting Curiosity and greed Tailgating Social pressure and politeness Quid pro quo Reciprocity Urgency and scarcity Fear and fear of missing out Consensus (social proof) Conformity

docs.title: 7.8 Defence tips
docs.text:
• "Trust but verify" — always confirm unusual requests through a completely separate, independently sourced contact channel
  • Security awareness training is not optional — 91% of all cyberattacks begin with a human element
  • Establish clear, unambiguous policies: IT will NEVER ask for passwords; executives will NEVER bypass financial controls by email
  • Create a culture where questioning suspicious requests is actively encouraged, not seen as rude or paranoid
  • Report ALL suspicious contacts to the security team immediately, even if you're not sure — others may have received the same approach

docs.title: 7.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Social engineers exploit authority, urgency, social proof, reciprocity, curiosity and scarcity.
  • The tactics are pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo, urgency and consensus.
  • Artificial urgency is the most reliable indicator of an attack: legitimate organisations give time to verify.
  • Defences are policies and culture: IT never asks for a password, unusual requests are verified through a separate channel, and reporting is encouraged.

docs.title: 7.10 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Match each tactic to the main psychological trigger: pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo, urgency, consensus.

    Answer

    Pretexting: authority and trust. Baiting: curiosity and greed. Tailgating: social pressure and politeness. Quid pro quo: reciprocity. Urgency: fear and fear of missing out. Consensus: conformity (social proof).

  2. A caller says he is from IT and needs your VPN password to push a security update. What do you do?

    Answer

    Refuse. Real IT departments never ask for a password. Hang up, find the IT department's number independently and call back, and report the attempt.

  3. Why is artificial urgency considered the most reliable sign of social engineering?

    Answer

    Urgency short-circuits rational thought, and legitimate organisations give you adequate time to verify. A demand for immediate action under threat should itself trigger suspicion.

  4. Describe the baiting USB experiment and the policy that follows.

    Answer

    A USB drive labelled "PAYROLL CONFIDENTIAL" is left in a car park; studies reported that between 45% and 60% of finders plugged it in. Policy: never plug in unknown drives, and disable AutoRun on all work computers.

  5. How can an organisation make tailgating less effective without relying on individual courage?

    Answer

    Provide mantraps or turnstiles that admit one person per badge, and set a clear policy that everyone without a visible, valid badge is challenged, backed by a culture where doing so is expected and not rude.

docs.title: Chapter 4: System and Operating-System Attacks
docs.text:
System and operating-system attacks go after the foundation under every application. If an attacker controls the operating system, the attacker controls everything that runs on it. This chapter covers buffer overflows, privilege escalation, rootkits, zero-day exploits, DLL hijacking and race conditions. Several of these are about getting more power than you were given, and several are about hiding once you have it.

Layman analogy

If the network is the road system and web applications are storefronts, the operating system is the building's foundation and structural frame. System attacks go after the foundation itself.

docs.title: 4.1 Buffer Overflow
docs.text:
A program allocates a fixed-size block of memory called a "buffer" (like a box of a specific size). If an attacker sends more data than the buffer can hold, the overflow writes into adjacent memory — including the program's execution instructions — allowing the attacker to redirect what the program does next.

Layman analogy

Imagine a form that says "Enter your name (maximum 10 characters)." You type 50 characters. The extra 40 spill over into the "next instruction" box and change what the programme does — now it runs YOUR instructions instead.

  • Stack-based overflow — overwrites the return address on the call stack, redirecting execution
  • Heap-based overflow — overwrites dynamically allocated memory structures
  • Return-to-libc — redirects execution to existing system library functions to avoid writing new shellcode

Example 4.1: Buffer Overflow

The Morris Worm (1988) — the first internet worm — exploited a buffer overflow in the Unix "fingerd" daemon. It self-replicated across the early internet, infecting ~6,000 machines (roughly 10% of all internet-connected computers at the time).

docs.title: 4.2 Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
An attacker who starts with limited, low-privilege access uses vulnerabilities to gain higher permissions — becoming an administrator or root user (the highest privilege level on a system).

  • Vertical Escalation — regular user gains administrator/root access
  • Horizontal Escalation — regular user accesses another user's data (same privilege, different account)

Common techniques:

  • Kernel exploits (e.g., "Dirty COW" CVE-2016-5195 — any Linux user could become root)
  • Misconfigured SUID binaries — programs that always run as root, regardless of who launches them
  • Unquoted service paths — Windows searches for executables in incorrect locations, allowing substitution

Example 4.2: Privilege Escalation

CVE-2021-4034 "PwnKit": A vulnerability in the polkit package present in virtually every Linux distribution for 12 years. Any local user could run a single command and instantly gain full root (administrator) access. Patched in January 2022.

docs.title: 4.3 Rootkits
docs.text:
Malware specifically engineered to hide its own presence — and the presence of other malware — from the operating system, antivirus software, and system administrators. Operates at the deepest levels of the system.

Layman analogy

Imagine hiring a corrupt building inspector who falsifies the inspection report to hide illegal construction. When you look at the blueprints (Task Manager, File Explorer), everything appears clean. The illegal rooms (malware) are there but completely hidden from official view.

  • Kernel-mode rootkits — run at the highest privilege level, modifying the OS kernel itself
  • User-mode rootkits — intercept API calls between applications and the kernel
  • Bootkits — load before the operating system even starts, invisible to any OS-level detection

Example 4.3: Rootkits

2005 — Sony BMG Music: Sony secretly installed a rootkit on millions of Windows PCs through commercially purchased music CDs. The rootkit hid itself and other files from the OS, created security vulnerabilities, and was installed without user consent. Sony faced massive legal action in multiple countries.

docs.title: 4.4 Zero-Day Exploits
docs.text:
A "zero-day" is a software vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor. Because it's unpatched, there is no defence available. Defenders have had "zero days" to fix it.

Layman analogy

Your house has a secret hidden entrance that even YOU don't know about. Burglars discover it first. Until you find it and seal it, your house is completely vulnerable no matter how many other locks and alarms you install.

  • Browser zero-days — attack through Chrome, Firefox, Safari while users simply browse the web
  • OS kernel zero-days — gain kernel-level control without any user interaction
  • Hardware firmware zero-days — persist even after complete OS reinstallation

Example 4.4: Zero-Day Exploits

Stuxnet (2010): A nation-state cyberweapon (attributed to the US and Israel) that used FOUR simultaneous Windows zero-days. It infiltrated Iranian nuclear facilities, destroyed centrifuges by causing them to spin at destructive speeds, while reporting completely normal operation to human operators. One of the most sophisticated cyber weapons ever publicly documented.

docs.title: 4.5 DLL Hijacking
docs.text:
Windows applications load Dynamic Link Libraries (DLLs) — shared code modules — by searching through folders in a specific order. If an attacker places a malicious DLL in a folder that is searched before the legitimate location, the malicious code runs instead.

Layman analogy

You ask your assistant to fetch "the Johnson contract." They check your desk first, then the filing cabinet. An attacker places a fake "Johnson contract" on your desk. Your assistant finds and acts on the fake one before ever reaching the legitimate filing cabinet.

  • Search order hijacking — place malicious DLL in the current directory or early in the PATH
  • DLL side-loading — place malicious DLL next to a legitimate, digitally signed application
  • Phantom DLL hijacking — create a DLL that an application tries to load but that doesn't yet exist

docs.title: 4.6 Race Condition (TOCTOU)
docs.text:
TOCTOU stands for Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use. An attacker exploits the tiny time gap between when a program checks a security condition and when it actually uses the resource — substituting something malicious in between.

Layman analogy

A nightclub bouncer checks your ID (Time of Check) and waves you forward to walk to the door (Time of Use). In the 2 seconds you walk, someone swaps your genuine wristband for a fake one. The door scanner sees the (now fake) wristband, not what the bouncer verified.

docs.title: 4.7 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Keep operating systems and all software fully updated with security patches
  • Apply the principle of least privilege — users and applications get only the minimum access they need
  • Use application whitelisting to prevent unauthorised programs from running
  • Deploy Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools for behavioural monitoring
  • Enable secure boot to protect against bootkits loading before the OS
  • Monitor system logs for unusual privilege escalation events

docs.title: 4.8 Summary
docs.text:
• A buffer overflow writes beyond a fixed block of memory and can redirect execution; privilege escalation gains more power than granted, vertically or horizontally.
  • Rootkits hide malware from the operating system, down to bootkits that load before it; zero-days exploit flaws the vendor does not yet know.
  • DLL hijacking abuses the order in which Windows searches for libraries; a race condition (TOCTOU) exploits the gap between a check and a use.
  • Defences: patching, least privilege, application whitelisting, EDR, secure boot and log monitoring.

docs.title: 4.9 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Explain how a stack-based buffer overflow can redirect a program.

    Answer

    The program copies input into a fixed-size buffer on the call stack. Too much input overruns the buffer and overwrites the saved return address next to it. When the function returns, execution jumps to the address the attacker placed there.

  2. Give an example of vertical and of horizontal privilege escalation.

    Answer

    Vertical: a regular user becomes root or administrator, for example through a kernel exploit such as Dirty COW or a misconfigured SUID program. Horizontal: a regular user reads or changes another regular user's data at the same privilege level.

  3. Why can antivirus running inside the operating system not find a bootkit?

    Answer

    A bootkit loads before the operating system starts, so it can alter what the operating system sees. Any scan that runs inside the compromised system relies on that altered view. Secure boot, which verifies the boot chain, is the countermeasure.

  4. Why is a zero-day vulnerability called "zero-day", and why is defence so hard?

    Answer

    The vendor has had zero days to fix it, because the flaw is unknown to the vendor. No patch exists, so patching cannot help until one is released. Defence relies on layers: least privilege, monitoring and segmentation.

  5. Describe a TOCTOU attack using a symbolic link and the principle that prevents it.

    Answer

    A privileged program checks that a file is harmless and then opens it. In the gap between check and use the attacker replaces the file with a symlink to a sensitive file, and the program acts on that. The principle is to make the check and the use a single atomic operation, so nothing can change in between.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Web Application Attacks
docs.text:
Almost everything we do online runs through a web application, which makes web applications among the most attacked systems in the world. This chapter covers six classic attacks: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery, path traversal, insecure file upload and insecure direct object references. All of them share one root cause: the application trusts input or requests that it should have checked. The OWASP Top 10 is the standard list of the most critical web security risks.

Layman analogy

A web application is like a shop with a front counter (the website) and a stockroom (the database and servers behind it). Web app attacks trick the counter staff into giving access to the stockroom, or sneak through doors that were left unlocked.

Figure 3.1. Where each web attack strikes: on the browser (XSS, CSRF), on the application (IDOR and broken authentication, file upload) and on the data behind it (SQL injection, path traversal).

docs.title: 3.1 SQL Injection (SQLi)
docs.text:
An attacker inserts malicious SQL (Structured Query Language) code into an input field — such as a login form, search box, or URL parameter — that the application then executes directly against its database.

Layman analogy

Imagine a restaurant where you order by writing on a form. If you write "Give me a burger. Also, show me every customer's credit card number," a poorly designed system reads the whole form as a command and complies.

How it works:

-- the legitimate query
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='alice' AND password='secret'

-- the query after the input  ' OR '1'='1'--  is pasted in
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1'-- ' AND password=''

The condition OR '1'='1' is always true, so all user records are returned. The attacker logs in as administrator.

Example 3.1: SQL Injection (SQLi)

2009 — Heartland Payment Systems: SQL injection was used to steal 130 million credit card numbers. The breach cost $140 million in settlements and is one of the largest in history.

Defence tip

Use parameterised queries / prepared statements. NEVER concatenate user input directly into SQL strings.

Why the injected query works

The application builds the query by pasting the input between quotes. The attacker's first quote closes the string early, OR '1'='1' adds a condition that is always true, and -- turns the rest of the line (the password check) into a comment. The database cannot tell which part of the text was written by the programmer and which by the attacker, because both arrive as one string.

The cure is to keep code and data apart. A parameterised query sends the SQL text and the values separately, so the input is never interpreted as SQL:

cur.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s AND password_hash = %s",
    (username, password_hash),
)

docs.title: 3.2 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text:
An attacker injects malicious JavaScript code into a web page. When other users view that page, the script executes in their browsers, potentially stealing session cookies, redirecting them to phishing sites, or logging their keystrokes.

Layman analogy

Imagine a public notice board where anyone can post messages. An attacker posts a message with a hidden script inside it. Every person who reads the board triggers the script in their own browser, which secretly sends their private data to the attacker.

  • Reflected XSS — malicious script is embedded in a URL and reflected back in the page response
  • Stored XSS — malicious script is saved in the database and served to every visitor who views that content
  • DOM-based XSS — client-side JavaScript writes attacker-controlled data to the page

Example 3.2: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

2014 — eBay XSS attack: Malicious product listings contained JavaScript that redirected buyers to phishing sites when they viewed the listing, stealing login credentials.

Defence tip

Sanitise and encode all user input before displaying it on a page. Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to restrict which scripts can run.

docs.title: 3.3 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
docs.text:
The attacker tricks an already-authenticated user's browser into making an unauthorised request to a website the user is logged into. The website thinks it's a legitimate action from the user.

Layman analogy

You're logged into your bank. An attacker sends you a link to a "funny cat photo" page. Hidden on that page is an invisible request to your bank: "Transfer $5,000 to account 99999." Your browser — already authenticated with the bank — automatically sends that request. The bank approves it, thinking you initiated it.

Example 3.3: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

2008 — YouTube CSRF vulnerability: Attackers could automatically add friends, change account settings, and add videos to favourites on any YouTube account simply by getting the victim to visit an attacker-controlled page.

Defence tip

Use CSRF tokens (unique, random values included in every form submission that the server verifies). Implement the SameSite cookie attribute to prevent cross-origin cookie sending.

docs.title: 3.4 Path / Directory Traversal
docs.text:
The attacker navigates outside the intended web folder using "../" sequences (which mean "go up one directory level"), reading sensitive system files that the web server should never expose.

Layman analogy

A hotel gives you a keycard to room 301. A traversal attack is like finding a maintenance corridor that connects your room — via multiple "go up one level" moves — to the master key cabinet in the manager's office.

An attack request looks like this:

https://example.com/files?name=../../../etc/passwd

This navigates three directory levels up from the web folder and reads the Linux system password file.

Example 3.4: Path / Directory Traversal

2019 — Pulse Secure VPN (CVE-2019-11510): A path traversal vulnerability allowed anyone — without any authentication — to retrieve credential files from the VPN server. This was actively exploited to breach hospitals and government agencies during the COVID-19 pandemic.

docs.title: 3.5 Insecure File Upload
docs.text:
The attacker uploads a malicious script disguised as a harmless file (like an image) to gain the ability to execute code on the server.

Layman analogy

You upload what appears to be a profile photo named "photo.jpg" — but it's actually a PHP script renamed with a .jpg extension. If the server doesn't properly verify file contents (only checking the extension), it stores the file. The attacker then browses to the file's URL, which executes the script and gives full server control.

Example 3.5: Insecure File Upload

Numerous WordPress plugin vulnerabilities have allowed attackers to upload PHP "webshells" disguised as image files, gaining complete control over the web server and all hosted websites.

docs.title: 3.6 IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference
docs.text:
The application uses predictable internal identifiers (like sequential numbers in a URL) to reference objects, but fails to verify whether the requesting user is actually authorised to access that specific object.

Layman analogy

A delivery app shows your order at the URL /orders/1001. You change it to /orders/1000 and see a stranger's full name, home address, and order contents. The server never checked whether order 1000 belongs to you.

Example 3.6: IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference

2019 — Instagram IDOR: Security researchers discovered they could access any user's private posts, stories, and account information simply by manipulating ID parameters in API requests.

docs.title: 3.7 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Validate and sanitise ALL user-supplied input on the server side — never trust client input
  • Use parameterised queries for all database operations to prevent SQL injection
  • Implement CSRF tokens on all forms that change data or perform actions
  • Validate file uploads by checking actual file content (magic bytes), not just file extension
  • Apply proper authorisation checks on every single API endpoint
  • Deploy a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to detect and block common attack patterns

docs.title: 3.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Web attacks exploit trust: the application trusts user input (SQLi, XSS, path traversal, file upload), trusts the browser's credentials (CSRF) or trusts identifiers it never checks (IDOR).
  • SQL injection is prevented by parameterised queries; XSS by encoding output and a Content Security Policy; CSRF by tokens and SameSite cookies.
  • Path traversal and insecure upload are prevented by validating paths and checking file content, not just the extension; IDOR by an authorisation check on every request.
  • A web application firewall helps, but cannot replace secure coding.

docs.title: 3.9 Exercises
docs.text:
1. A login query is built as SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='\(u' AND password='\)p'. The attacker enters ' OR '1'='1'-- as the username. Write the resulting query and explain why it returns every user.

    Answer

    The query becomes SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1'-- ' AND password=''. The condition '1'='1' is always true, and -- turns the rest of the line into a comment, so the password check disappears. Every row matches and the attacker is logged in, often as the first (administrator) record.

  2. Distinguish reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS.

    Answer

    Reflected: the script is in a link and is reflected back in the page response. Stored: the script is saved in the database and served to every visitor who views that content. DOM-based: client-side JavaScript writes attacker-controlled data into the page.

  3. Why does CSRF succeed even though the attacker never sees the victim's cookie? Name two defences.

    Answer

    The victim's browser automatically attaches its authenticated session cookie to any request to the bank, including one triggered by a hidden form or image on the attacker's page. The server cannot tell the request was not intended. Defences: unique CSRF tokens checked by the server, and the SameSite cookie attribute.

  4. A site shows your invoice at /invoice?id=2041. Changing the number to 2040 shows another customer's invoice. Name the flaw and the fix.

    Answer

    This is an insecure direct object reference (IDOR). The fix is an authorisation check on every request, confirming that the logged-in user owns the invoice, and not relying on the identifier being hard to guess.

  5. Why is checking the file extension not enough to make an upload safe?

    Answer

    An attacker can rename a PHP script to shell.jpg. If the server only checks the extension it stores the file, and requesting it can execute the code. Validate the actual content (magic bytes), store uploads outside the web root, and do not allow them to execute.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Wireless and Contactless Attacks
docs.text:
A wired connection must be physically tapped; a wireless one can be heard by anyone within range of the right receiver. This chapter covers six attacks on Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and contactless cards: evil twin access points, WPS PIN attacks, WPA2 handshake cracking, deauthentication, Bluetooth attacks and RFID or NFC cloning.

Layman analogy

A wired network connection is like a private phone call on a landline — physically intercepting it requires access to the line. A wireless network is like a conversation on a walkie-talkie — anyone with the right receiver within range can listen in.

docs.title: 10.1 Evil Twin Access Point
docs.text:
The attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi access point with the same name (SSID) as a legitimate network. Users connect to the attacker's hotspot thinking it's real. All their internet traffic flows through the attacker's device.

How it works:

  • Attacker sets up a hotspot named "Heathrow Airport Free WiFi" at an airport
  • Victims' devices connect automatically or users select it thinking it's legitimate
  • Attacker intercepts all traffic: login credentials, session cookies, browsing history, banking data

Example 10.1: Evil Twin Access Point

2024 — Australian Federal Police: A man was charged after using a portable Evil Twin device on multiple domestic flights, capturing passenger credentials. He used a laptop and a portable wireless device to create fake "Free Inflight WiFi" networks.

docs.title: 10.2 WPS PIN Attack
docs.text:
Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) was designed to make router configuration easy — users could connect new devices via an 8-digit PIN. A critical design flaw allows the PIN to be tested in two separate parts (the first four digits, then the next three, since the eighth digit is only a checksum), reducing the search space from 100 million combinations to just 11,000.

Impact: Any WPA2 router with WPS enabled can be cracked in approximately 4 hours, regardless of how complex the WPA2 password is.

Defence tip

Disable WPS completely on your router. The convenience is not worth the security risk.

docs.title: 10.3 WPA2 Handshake Capture and Cracking
docs.text:
When any device connects to a WPA2 network, a "4-way handshake" authentication exchange occurs. An attacker captures this handshake (either by waiting, or by sending deauthentication packets to force devices to reconnect), then performs an offline brute-force or dictionary attack against the captured data.

  • Step 1: Send deauthentication packets to force a client to reconnect
  • Step 2: Capture the 4-way handshake from the reconnection
  • Step 3: Run Hashcat with GPU acceleration and wordlists against the captured handshake

Weak passwords like "password123" or "ourwifi2024" can be cracked against a captured handshake in seconds using GPU-accelerated tools.

Defence tip

Use WPA3 (uses SAE protocol — Simultaneous Authentication of Equals — which is resistant to offline dictionary attacks). Use a complex, random Wi-Fi password of 20+ characters.

docs.title: 10.4 Deauthentication Attack
docs.text:
The 802.11 Wi-Fi standard includes management frames for controlling connections. An attacker sends spoofed deauthentication frames (in the original standard, these are unauthenticated) that tell clients they have been disconnected from the access point, forcibly kicking them off the network.

  • Used to capture WPA2 handshakes (as above)
  • Used as a standalone DoS attack — continuously kicking users off the network

Defence tip

WPA3 implements Protected Management Frames (PMF), which cryptographically authenticate deauthentication packets, making this attack ineffective.

docs.title: 10.5 Bluetooth Attacks
docs.text:
BlueSnarfing: Unauthorised access to a Bluetooth-enabled device to steal data: contacts, calendar entries, messages, photos.

BlueJacking: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices (more of an annoyance than a security threat).

BlueBorne: A critical set of Bluetooth vulnerabilities (2017) allowing Remote Code Execution (RCE) on affected devices with NO pairing required and NO user interaction needed.

Example 10.5: Bluetooth Attacks

BlueBorne (2017): Affected 8.2 billion devices running Android, iOS, Windows, and Linux. An attacker within Bluetooth range could silently take complete control of vulnerable devices without any user action, prompt, or pairing request.

Defence tip

Keep Bluetooth turned off when not actively using it. Apply security patches to all devices promptly — Bluetooth patches are among the most critical.

docs.title: 10.6 RFID / NFC Cloning
docs.text:
RFID (Radio-Frequency Identification) and NFC (Near-Field Communication) are used in hotel key cards, corporate access badges, transit cards, passports, and contactless payment cards. Attackers use inexpensive, commercially available hardware to silently clone these cards.

Layman analogy

An attacker walks past you in a lift or in a queue carrying a concealed reader. In the time it takes to ride two floors, they've read and cloned your access badge. They now have a perfect copy that grants them access to the same areas as you.

Example 10.6: RFID / NFC Cloning

2014: Security researchers demonstrated cloning corporate RFID access badges from 3 feet away using $20 worth of off-the-shelf components — showing the attack is trivially accessible to any motivated attacker.

Defence tip

Use RFID-blocking wallets or card sleeves for your access badges and contactless payment cards. Organisations should upgrade to cryptographically secure card systems (MIFARE DESFire EV2 or later).

docs.title: 10.7 Tools and defences at a glance
docs.text:
As in the previous chapter, the tools are used both by attackers and by defenders testing their own networks.

Attack Tools seen in the literature Typical defence Evil twin access point airbase-ng, WiFi Pineapple VPN; do not trust open networks WPS PIN attack Reaver, Bully Disable WPS WPA2 handshake cracking aircrack-ng, Hashcat, hcxdumptool WPA3; long random passphrase Deauthentication aireplay-ng, MDK3, mdk4 WPA3 protected management frames Bluetooth attacks BlueZ, hciconfig, bettercap Turn Bluetooth off; patch RFID and NFC cloning Proxmark3, Flipper Zero, ACR122U Blocking sleeves; secure card systems

docs.title: 10.8 Defence tips
docs.text:
• Disable WPS on your home and office routers immediately

docs.title: 10.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Wireless signals can be heard by anyone in range, so attackers need no physical access.
  • Evil twin hotspots intercept traffic; WPS PIN attacks reduce 100 million combinations to 11,000; handshake capture allows offline cracking; deauthentication knocks clients off.
  • Bluetooth attacks include BlueSnarfing, BlueJacking and BlueBorne; RFID and NFC cards can be cloned with cheap hardware.
  • Defences: disable WPS, use WPA3 (SAE and protected management frames), use a VPN, turn Bluetooth off when unused and upgrade to cryptographically secure cards.

docs.title: 10.10 Exercises
docs.text:
1. A WPS PIN has 8 digits, but the last is a checksum. The router confirms the first four digits and the next three separately. How many guesses are needed in the worst case, compared with \(10^8\)?

    Answer

    The first part has \(10^4=10{,}000\) possibilities and the second has \(10^3=1{,}000\), so at most \(11{,}000\) guesses instead of 100 million, about 9,000 times fewer.

  2. How does WPA3 help against handshake cracking and deauthentication?

    Answer

    WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake. It also implements Protected Management Frames, which authenticate deauthentication frames and make spoofed ones ineffective.

  3. You are asked to join "Heathrow Airport Free WiFi". How might it be an evil twin, and what should you do?

    Answer

    An attacker can create a hotspot with the same name, and devices that connect automatically or by choice send all their traffic through the attacker. Confirm the network name with airport staff, avoid sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi, and always use a VPN.

  4. Why is cloning an RFID access badge so easy, and what is the remedy?

    Answer

    Older cards respond to any reader with a fixed identifier that cheap hardware can read and copy from a short distance. Remedies: RFID-blocking sleeves for the cards, and for organisations an upgrade to cryptographically secure card systems.

  5. Name three good practices for Bluetooth.

    Answer

    Turn Bluetooth off when you are not using it, apply security patches promptly (BlueBorne needed no pairing and no user action), and do not accept unexpected pairing requests.
